title: Bidirectional regulation of social memory by two distinct types of GABAergic neurons in the lateral septum

paper_content.abstract: Humans and animals memorize and recognize familiar conspecifics during social interactions, known as social memory. While the hippocampus is crucial for social memory, the dynamic regulation of social memory remains unclear. Here, using male mice, we identified two molecularly distinct subpopulations of GABAergic neurons in the mouse lateral septum (LS) expressing somatostatin (SST) and calbindin 1 (CB), respectively, with complementary distribution patterns. Activation of SST+ neurons enhances social memory acquisition, whereas activation of CB+ neurons inhibits it. Optogenetic manipulation of SST+ neurons regulates theta oscillations, correlating with their impact on social memory. SST+-dLS neurons and CB+-vLS neurons preferentially receive stronger excitatory inputs from the dorsal (vCA1d) and ventral (vCA1v) parts of vCA1, respectively. Functionally, the vCA1d→SST+-dLS→lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) circuit promotes social memory acquisition, whereas the vCA1v→CB+-vLS→anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN) pathway suppresses it. This study uncovers two parallel neural circuits underpinning the dynamic regulation of social memory in male mice.
paper_content.introduction:
Social behaviors encompass a range of interactions between conspecifics and involve continuous integration of acute sensory inputs, internal social states, and decision-making1. Internal social states, combined with emotion and memory, provide the basis for transforming sensory inputs into behavioral decisions1. During social interactions, animals can memorize and recognize familiar conspecifics2. This social recognition memory is an important cue for determining forms of social behavior, i.e. social approach or avoidance2. Deficits in social memory are commonly observed in neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases3,4. Previous studies have identified several hippocampal subregions—including dorsal CA2 (dCA2)2,5,6, dorsal CA3 (dCA3)7,8, ventral CA1 (vCA1) neurons9-14—and their synaptic connections15-20, as being critical for social memory. However, the dynamic regulation of social memory outside the hippocampus remains to be elucidated. Anatomical and functional studies suggest that the vCA1 sends many axonal branches and forms strong functional connections with the lateral septum (LS)21,22. Early studies also suggest that interfering with vasopressin and oxytocin signaling in the LS modulates social recognition memory23-27. In addition, excitatory synaptic inputs from dCA3 and inhibitory synaptic inputs from medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) to the the dorsal LS (dLS) have been implicated in social memory regulation7,20. However, deletion of G-protein coupled metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) in the LS or silencing of dopamine receptor 3 (Drd3)+-LS neurons impaired sociability without affecting social novelty preference28,29. In contrast, deletion of the oxytocin receptor (Oxtr) did not affect sociability but significantly impaired preference for social novelty28, highlighting the functional heterogeneity of the LS in regulating distinct aspects of social behaviors. These findings suggest that the LS contains molecularly and functionally heterogeneous subcircuits that contribute to different aspects of social behaviors30. Therefore, it remains unclear how social behavior is regulated by different LS subcircuits and how their synaptic strength is shaped by social experience.

More than 90% of LS neurons are GABAergic31,32. Previous studies have indicated that LS neurons express different molecular markers, i.e., somatostatin (SST), neurotensin (NTS), calbindin 1 (Calb1 or CB), calretinin (CR), Oxtr, Drd3, adenosine A receptors (A R), and type 2 corticotropin-releasing factor receptor (Crfr2)29,31,33-39. Increasing evidence suggests that different subsets of LS neurons are engaged in distinct animal behaviors. For example, activation of Crfr2+ or Oxtr+ neurons can promote anxiety levels in mice34,40, while the NTS+-LS→hypothalamic tuberal nucleus (TU) and NTS+-LS→anterior hypothalamic nucleus (AHN) pathways can regulate hedonic feeding and social trauma37,38, respectively. In addition, CA2→LS and LS→ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) projections are implicated in social aggressive behaviors32,41. Arginine-vasopressin (AVP) released from bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (BNST) terminals in the LS may facilitate social aggression by modulating CA2→dLS synapses42. Recent transcriptomic studies identified multiple molecular distinct neuronal clusters in the LS43,44,45,46,47,48. However, it is uncertain whether LS neuronal subsets defined by molecular markers represent functionally distinct subcircuits in regulating social behaviors30. Given the broad behavioral roles of LS, several models have been proposed to explain its circuit heterogeneity. Besnard and Leroy proposed that parallel LS subcircuits may function as independent units, each receiving inputs from and sending outputs to distinct brain regions to regulate specific behavioral states30. Since most LS neurons are GABAergic31,32, lateral inhibition may further shape interactions between these units. However, it remains unclear how LS subpopulations are defined, spatially or molecularly separated, and how different neuronal clusters dynamically regulate social behaviors.

In the present study, we identified two distinct subpopulations of GABAergic neurons in the LS, that express SST and CB, respectively. Both types of neurons respond to socially relevant sensory stimuli, suggesting a potential role in social behaviors. Interestingly, we found that SST+ neurons are necessary and sufficient for social memory acquisition, whereas activation of CB+ neurons inhibits it. Furthermore, SST+ neurons play an essential role in the regulation of the theta rhythm oscillations that emerge during social memory acquisition. In addition, social memory acquisition selectively potentiates synaptic connections to SST+-dLS neurons. Importantly, we discovered two parallel pathways with distinct effects: the vCA1d→SST+-dLS→lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) circuit promotes social memory, whereas the vCA1v→CB+-vLS→AHN circuit reduces it. Thus, our study highlights two parallel subcortical neural circuits that underpins social memory acquisition, demonstrating that social memory expression is dynamically modulated by two parallel subcircuits in the LS.
paper_content.results:
Identification of neuronal subpopulations in the LS

Here, to reveal the cellular composition of the LS, we used single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) and analyzed the transcriptomes of 21 023 nuclei (Supplementary Fig. 1). Based on clustering analysis, we identified non-neuronal cells as well as GABAergic (Slc32a1+) and glutamatergic (Slc17a6+) neurons (Supplementary Fig. 1 and 2), which likely originated from the nearby medial septum49. After excluding non-neuronal cell types and nearby non-LS neurons, GABAergic neurons in the LS were clustered into nine neuronal subpopulations (Fig. 1a; Supplementary Fig. 1 and 2). Seven of these clusters (#6, #7, #8, #9, #10, #13, #14) corresponded to previously reported LS neuronal populations43,44,45,46,47,48. Specifically, cluster #6 aligned with neurons expressing Pax643,44,45, or Wnt5a46; cluster #7 with Crhr2-expressing neurons43,44,45; clusters #8 and #9 with Drd2- and Rai14-expressing populations43; cluster #10 with neurons expressing Rnf20744 or MYO5B47; cluster #13 with neurons expressing Ntf343or Slc18a245; cluster #14 with populations defined by Nts43,48, Sst45, or Hs3st247. Among these clusters, SST+ and Calb1+ (CB+) neurons are of particular interest because both are widely used molecular markers of functionally distinct neuronal types in the neocortex, thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), and elsewhere50,51. To test whether SST+ and CB+ neurons also represent two distinct neuronal subtypes in the LS, we analyzed the transcriptional profiles of both neuronal subpopulations. Indeed, SST+ and CB+ neurons in the LS showed distinct molecular profiles, with SST+ neurons specifically expressing neurotensin (Nts) and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (Glp1r), and CB+ neurons specifically expressing serotonin 2c receptor (Htr2c) and prolactin receptor (Prlr) (Fig. 1b, c). To validate these findings, we performed additional RNAscope in situ hybridization. Consistent with the snRNA-seq results, 65.69% ± 0.92% of Sst+ neurons co-expressed Glp1r and 52.55% ± 2.40% of Sst + neurons co-expressed Nts (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b). In contrast, 70.52% ± 1.37% of Calb1+ neurons co-expressed Htr2c, and 81.53 % ± 3.50 % of Calb1+ neurons co-expressed Prlr (Supplementary Fig. 3c, d). These data suggest that SST+ and CB+ neurons represent two molecularly distinct subpopulations.

To study the functions of LS SST+ and CB+ neurons, we used SST-Cre and CB-Cre mice to label the two subpopulations. We performed single-molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization (smFISH) against Sst in LS slices from SST-Cre/LSL-H2B-GFP (SST-H2B-GFP) mice expressing nucleus-localized green fluorescent protein (GFP) in SST+ neurons and confirmed the specificity of SST-Cre mice (Supplementary Fig. 4a, b). Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining against CB in CB-Cre/Ai14 mice expressing tdTomato in CB+ neurons also revealed high specificity (Supplementary Fig. 4c, d).

The LS can be divided into dorsal, ventral, and intermediate subregions (dLS, vLS, and iLS, respectively). To capture the finer spatial distribution patterns of SST+ and CB+ neurons in the LS, we performed IHC staining for CB and NeuN in brain sections from SST-Cre/Ai14 (SST-Ai14) mice expressing tdTomato in SST+ neurons. Notably, two largely non-overlapping subpopulations of neurons (SST+ and CB+) were identified in the LS (Fig. 1d, e). Surprisingly, the SST+ and CB+ neurons showed complementary patterns in the three subregions (Fig. 1d; Supplementary Fig. 5); i.e., high SST+ neuronal density in the dLS, but high CB+ neuronal density in the iLS/vLS (Fig. 1d; Supplementary Fig. 5). In total, 25.18% ± 1.05% of LS neurons expressed SST, 21.55% ± 1.46% of neurons expressed CB and 1.70% ± 0.15% expressed both (Fig. 1f). We next examined their distribution along the anterior–posterior LS axis. The proportion of SST+ neurons decreased gradually from anterior to posterior, while CB+ neurons showed the opposite trend (Fig. 1g-i; Supplementary Fig. 5). Because neurons expressing estrogen receptor 1 (Esr1+) neurons have been identified as a distinct functional unit in the vLS43, we asked whether they correspond to CB⁺ neurons in this region. To address this, we performed immunostaining for CB in Esr1-Cre/Ai14 (Esr1-Ai14) mice (Supplementary Fig. 6). We found that 27.53% ± 0.97% of tdTomato+ neurons co-expressed CB, and 12.01% ± 1.93% of CB+ neurons co-expressed tdTomato, indicating that Esr1+ and CB+ neurons in the vLS only partially overlap and likely represent distinct molecular subpopulations.

To test whether SST+ and CB+ neurons have different morphological or electrophysiological properties, we recorded 10 SST+ and 11 CB+ neurons using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in LS slices prepared from SST-Ai14 and CB-Ai14 mice, respectively, and reconstructed their morphology using biocytin-avidin labeling (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Group analyses showed that CB+ neurons had smaller somata compared to SST+ neurons, but similar dendritic and axonal complexity (Supplementary Fig. 7b-d). Both neurons showed comparable excitability (Supplementary Fig. 7e-f), although CB+ neurons had larger sag amplitudes, mediated by hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels52 (Supplementary Fig. 7g, h). The snRNA-seq results also indicated that CB+ neurons expressed a higher level of Hcn1 (Supplementary Fig. 7i), confirming more functional HCN channels.

Together, our results indicate that SST+ and CB+ neurons represent two unique functional units with complementary distribution patterns, distinct molecular profiles and electrophysiological properties. Therefore, we decided to focus on these two neuronal populations in the following studies.

SST+ and CB+ neurons actively engage in social interactions

To determine whether SST+ and CB+ neurons respond to social behaviors, we performed immunohistochemical staining for c-fos, a marker of neuronal activation (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Notably, 10-min social interaction significantly activated LS neurons (Supplementary Fig. 8b). The social stimulus increased the densities of c-fos+/SST+ neurons in all three subregions, while primarily affecting c-fos+/CB+ neurons in the iLS/vLS (Supplementary Fig. 8c-e). These results indicate that both SST+ and CB+ neurons are recruited during social interactions, with distinct activation patterns.

To examine their firing properties, we performed in-vivo electrophysiology to monitor single-neuron spiking activity when the subject mouse investigated a confined stranger mouse for 5 min (Supplementary Fig. 9a, b). We unilaterally injected a Cre-dependent AAV expressing light-sensitive hyperpolarizing opsin archaerhodopsin (ArchT) and tdTomato (AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato) into the LS of SST-Cre and CB-Cre mice, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 9a). Using optogenetic tagging (see Methods), we delivered 532-nm light to identify ArchT-positive neurons (Supplementary Fig. 9c-e). Among SST⁺ neurons, 44.4% (8/18) displayed a significant increase in firing rate compared to the baseline period, while 11.1% (2/18) displayed a significant reduction in firing rate (Supplementary Fig. 9g). On average, SST+ neurons had a significantly higher firing rate during social interaction (Supplementary Fig. 9f; 9g, right), consistent with the increased number of c-fos+/SST+ neurons (Supplementary Fig. 8). In contrast, CB⁺ neurons displayed more heterogeneous responses: 20% (4/20) increased and 20% (4/20) decreased their firing rates, resulting in no overall population change (Supplementary Fig. 9h, i).

To characterize the temporal dynamics of single-unit activity of SST+ neurons in a more controllable social context, head-fixed subject mice were allowed to run freely on a previously established running wheel53 while exposed to an anesthetized stranger or a novel object (Supplementary Fig. 9j). Most SST+ neurons (63.64%, 14/22) increased firing in response to the anesthetized stranger, whereas fewer SST+ neurons (18.18%, 4/22) responded to the novel object (Supplementary Fig. 9k). At the population level, responses to the stranger were significantly stronger than those to the object (Supplementary Fig. 9l-m).

Together, these findings show that both SST+ and CB+ neurons in the LS respond during social interactions, but SST+ neurons are more strongly activated.

Activation of SST+ neurons enhances social memory acquisition

Considering the active engagement of SST+ and CB+ neurons in social interactions (Supplementary Fig. 8 and Fig. 9), we next explored their roles in regulating social behaviors using the classical three-chamber social test (Fig. 2a). To silence SST+ neurons, we bilaterally injected a Cre-dependent AAV expressing TeNT (tetanus neurotoxin, light chain) and enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP) (AAV-DIO-EGFP-2A-TeNT) into the LS of SST-Cre mice (SST-TeNT group, Fig. 2b). We found that TeNT silencing of SST+ neurons did not alter the locomotion in the open field test (OFT) (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b), but it significantly reduced anxiety levels in the elevated plus maze (EPM) (Supplementary Fig. 10c, d), similar with the anxiogenic effects of activating LS Crfr2+ neurons34. Moreover, SST-TeNT mice exhibited normal sociability (Supplementary Fig. 10e), but impaired social novelty preference compared to the control mice (Fig. 2c). A social discrimination (SD) index was calculated for each mouse to enable direct comparison of mice within different groups. The SD index in the SST-TeNT mice decreased markedly, suggesting an impairment in social novelty preference (Fig. 2c). Furthermore, the SST-TeNT mice showed normal preference for the novel object compared to the familiar object upon presentation (Supplementary Fig. 10f, g), suggesting normal recognition. Social novelty preference relies on the social memory of the familiar mice, enabling discrimination between novel and familiar mice during social novelty test9. To test whether TeNT blockade of SST+ neurons abolished social memory, we next performed a classic five-trial social memory test2 (Fig. 2d). As previously reported, the control mice showed normal social memory in trials 2-4, as indicated by a decrease in the time spent interacting with the now familiar mouse, but in trial 5 the duration of interactions with a novel mouse recovered to baseline levels (Fig. 2e). In contrast, the SST-TeNT mice showed impaired habituation to the familiar mouse, as indicated by equal interaction times for trials 1-5 (Fig. 2e), thus confirming the necessity of SST+-LS neurons for social memory.

To determine whether SST+ neurons are required for social memory acquisition and/or recall, we injected AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato (SST-ArchT) or AAV-DIO-tdTomato alone (Control) into the LS of SST-Cre mice. We then delivered a green laser (532 nm) during memory acquisition or recall (Fig. 2f, g). Patch-clamp recordings confirmed that green light effectively suppressed SST neuronal firing (Supplementary Fig. 11a). Inhibition of SST+ neurons via ArchT during the memory acquisition phase disrupted social memory (Fig. 2h; Supplementary Fig. 11b), whereas light delivery during the memory recall phase had no effect (Fig. 2i). Baseline sociability remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 11c, d). To further confirm that SST+ neurons are specifically required during social memory acquisition, we repeated this experiment with two rounds of acquisition and recall. We found that optogenetic silencing of SST+ neurons during the first acquisition disrupted the mouse’s ability to distinguish between S1 and S2. This disruption also extended to the next round, impairing discrimination between S3 and S4 (Supplementary Fig. 12). These results further support that SST+ neuron activity is essential for the acquisition—but not the recall—of social memory. Furthermore, optogenetic stimulation did not elicit significant real-time place preference (Supplementary Fig. 11e), confirming that inhibition of SST+ neurons did not produce rewarding or aversive effects.

To determine whether activation of SST+ neurons during memory acquisition is sufficient for enhancing social memory, we applied a more challenging social memory task. First, we performed social memory recall with a 0–60-min interval after memory acquisition and found that social memory gradually decreased as the interval increased (Supplementary Fig. 11g). We then used a 40-min interval, under which control mice barely discriminated between familiar and novel mice (Supplementary Fig. 11g). Afterwards, we expressed Cre-dependent depolarizing opsin channelrhodopsin (ChR2) in SST+ neurons (Fig. 2j). Patch-clamp recordings confirmed that 473-nm laser pulses reliably evoked action potentials in SST+ neurons at multiple frequencies (Fig. 2k). Optogenetic activation of SST+ neurons did not change baseline sociability (Supplementary Fig. 11f), but significantly enhanced social memory recall 40 min later (Fig. 2l). Therefore, activation of SST+ neurons is both necessary and sufficient for social memory acquisition.

SST+ neurons regulate social-related theta oscillations

To investigate how SST⁺ neurons influence social memory acquisition, we examined local field potential (LFP) dynamics in the LS during social interaction. LFPs were recorded in freely moving C57BL/6 mice during a 20‑min session with a single stranger mouse to avoid confounds from switching between different conspecifics (Fig. 3a-c). We observed a significant increase in the spectral power of theta rhythm oscillations (4–12 Hz) during all four periods (P1–P4) (Fig. 3d, e), but no change in the power of other bands (1–3, 13–30, and 31–80 Hz) (Fig. 3e). Theta power remained elevated during both social bouts and non-social intervals (Fig. 3d, e), suggesting a sustained change in network state rather than a transient sensory response. Given the importance of theta oscillations in memory encoding and retrieval54,55, these findings suggest that theta enhancement is a potential mechanism for social memory acquisition.

Theta oscillations are shaped by cell-type-specific firing patterns, with GABAergic neurons often playing a key role56,57. To determine whether SST⁺ neuron activity is coupled to theta rhythms, we performed simultaneous LFP and single-unit recordings from optogenetically tagged SST⁺ neurons during social interaction (Fig. 3a; Supplementary Fig. 9a-d). We analyzed the temporal firing patterns of SST+ neurons during theta oscillations (Fig. 3f). The Rayleigh test was applied to determine whether SST neuronal spikes were significantly locked to theta phases58,59 (Fig. 3g). Similar to LFP activity, the proportion of significantly phase-locked SST+ neurons increased markedly (Fig. 3h). Group analysis indicated that SST+ neurons preferentially fired during the descending phase of theta oscillations (Fig. 3i), suggesting they are actively engaged in shaping theta activity. In line with this, a recent study demonstrated that vCA1 neurons encode social stimuli using both firing rate and theta-phase coding60, Together, these findings suggest that theta-phase–locked firing of SST⁺ neurons may provide a temporal framework for social memory acquisition.

To test whether theta enhancement is specific to social contexts, we compared theta power across three conditions: 10‑min social interaction, 20-min exploration of empty chamber, and 10-min exploration of a novel object (Supplementary Fig. 13a). Theta power selectively increased during social interaction, emerging within the second 2 min and persisting throughout stimulus presence (Supplementary Fig. 13b). In contrast, theta power remained at baseline during non‑social conditions. However, the proportion of phase-locked SST+ neurons stayed elevated even in non‑social conditions (Supplementary Fig. 13c). Together, these results indicate that theta oscillation enhancement is context-dependent.

To elucidate whether SST+ neurons are required for social-related theta oscillations, we bilaterally injected AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato and implanted an LFP-recording optrode into the LS of SST-Cre mice (Fig. 3j). ArchT-silencing of SST+ neurons blocked the increase in theta oscillation power (Fig. 3k), suggesting that activation of SST+ neurons is necessary for theta oscillations. Conversely, to test if SST+ neurons can drive theta oscillations, we bilaterally injected AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP and implanted an LFP-recording optrode into the LS of SST-Cre mice (Fig. 3l). Optogenetic theta-frequency stimulation of SST+ neurons enhanced theta oscillation power in the open field chamber (Fig. 3m), highlighting the role of SST+ neurons in driving theta oscillations.

We next explored the synaptic mechanism underlying this effect. Feedback inhibition from GABAergic neurons is thought to promote rhythm oscillations59,61,62. To examine local connectivity, we injected AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP into the LS of SST-Cre/Ai14 mice and performed patch-clamp recordings from tdTomato-negative LS neurons in acute slices (Fig. 3n, o). In the presence of tetrodotoxin (TTX) and 4-aminopyridine (4-AP), all recorded SST⁻ neurons (38/38) exhibited monosynaptic inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) in response to laser stimulation (Fig. 3p, q). These IPSCs were abolished by the GABA receptor antagonist (PTX) but unaffected by glutamate receptor antagonists (CNQX and D-AP5), confirming GABAergic transmission (Fig. 3p, q). These results demonstrated that SST+ neurons directly inhibit other neurons in the LS. Combined with the extensive local axonal arborizations of SST⁺ neurons (Supplementary Fig. 7a, d). these results suggest that SST⁺ neurons provide recurrent inhibition, supporting theta oscillations within the LS59,62.

Activation of CB+ neurons suppresses social memory acquisition

As shown above, both SST+ and CB+ neurons actively engage in social interactions (Supplementary Fig. 8). To determine the role of CB+ neurons in social behaviors, we employed a chemogenetic approach to activate these neurons. We injected a Cre-dependent AAV expressing mCherry-tagged hM3Dq, a designer receptor exclusively activated by designer drugs (DREADD)63, into the LS of CB-Cre mice (Supplementary Fig. 14a). Patch-clamp recordings confirmed that clozapine-N-oxide (CNO), a DREADD activator, significantly depolarized the membrane potential and increased the firing rate of hM3Dq-expressing neurons (Supplementary Fig. 14b, c). After 3 weeks of recovery, we intraperitoneally (i.p.) injected CNO 30 min before behavioral tests (Supplementary Fig. 14h). Chemogenetic activation of CB+ neurons did not alter baseline locomotion, anxiety or novel object preference (Supplementary Fig. 14d-g, o-q, t). The two control groups, i.e., control and CB-hM3Dq mice receiving saline injection, exhibited normal sociability and social memory (Supplementary Fig. 14i, j, r, s). In contrast, the CNO-injected CB-hM3Dq mice exhibited significantly impaired social memory, with no change in baseline sociability (Supplementary Fig. 14i, j). In the five-trial social memory test, the CNO-injected CB-hM3Dq mice showed impaired social memory as indicated by equal interaction times for trials 1-5 (Supplementary Fig. 14k), confirming that chemogenetic activation of CB+-LS neurons blocked social memory.

To address whether CB+ neurons are crucial for social memory acquisition and/or social memory recall, we bilaterally injected AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP (CB-ChR2) or AAV-DIO-EYFP alone (Control) into the LS of CB-Cre mice (Fig. 4a), then delivered blue laser pulses during memory acquisition or recall (Fig. 4b, c). ChR2 activation of CB+ neurons did not change baseline sociability (Supplementary Fig. 14l, m). However, optogenetic activation of CB+ neurons during the memory acquisition phase significantly impaired social memory, whereas activation during the memory recall phase did not impact social memory at all (Fig. 4b, c).

To test whether inhibition of CB+ neurons influences social memory, we bilaterally injected AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato (CB-ArchT) or AAV-DIO-tdTomato alone (Control) into the LS of CB-Cre mice (Fig. 4d). ArchT inhibition of CB+ neurons did not change baseline sociability or real-time place preference (Fig. 4e; Supplementary Fig. 14n). However, compared to the control mice, optogenetic inhibition of CB+ neurons during social memory acquisition improved social memory recall after a 40-min interval (Fig. 4f), mimicking the effect of SST⁺ neuron activation (Fig. 2l). Together, these results reveal a bidirectional relationship in which SST⁺ neurons facilitate, and CB⁺ neurons suppress, social memory acquisition.

Mutual inhibition between SST⁺ and CB⁺ neurons

Given the opposite effect on social memory, we hypothesized that CB+ neurons may inhibit SST+ neurons in the LS. To test this, we bilaterally injected AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP and AAV-fDIO-H2B-mCherry into the LS of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice and recorded SST+ neurons (mCherry+) in LS slices (Fig. 4g, h). Light stimulation evoked IPSCs in all recorded SST⁺ neurons (32/32), indicating widespread CB⁺→SST⁺ connectivity (Fig. 4i, j). Perfusion of TTX/4-AP and PTX confirmed these connections were monosynaptic and GABAergic (Fig. 4i, j). To determine whether SST⁺ neurons reciprocally inhibit CB⁺ neurons, we expressed ChR2 in SST⁺ neurons and H2B-mCherry in CB⁺ neurons of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice (Supplementary Fig. 15a, b). Light stimulation elicited IPSCs in all recorded CB⁺ neurons (26/26), which were abolished by TTX/4-AP and PTX, confirming monosynaptic SST⁺→CB⁺ inhibition (Supplementary Fig. 15c, d).

To assess whether these reciprocal interactions occur in vivo, we employed opto-tagging to isolate single units of SST⁺ and CB⁺ neurons. We injected AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato unilaterally into the LS of SST-Cre and CB-Cre mice, and conducted optrode recording in these head-fixed animals (Supplementary Fig. 16a, b). Spike waveform analysis revealed that SST+ neurons have longer trough-to-peak durations, wider half-width, and larger peak-trough ratios than CB+ neurons (Supplementary Fig. 16c, d). Using these features, we identified putative CB⁺ (pCB⁺) neurons in SST-ArchT mice and putative SST⁺ (pSST⁺) neurons in CB-ArchT mice.

To mimic social interaction, head-fixed mice were presented with an anesthetized stranger (Supplementary Fig. 16b). We identified 15 pCB+ neurons and 14 pSST+ neurons from recordings in SST-ArchT and CB-ArchT mice, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 16d). Silencing SST⁺ neurons increased firing in 5 of 15 pCB⁺ neurons at baseline and in 12 of 15 pCB⁺ neurons during social stimulus presentation (Supplementary Fig. 16e-g), suggesting that SST⁺ neurons exert stronger inhibition on CB⁺ neurons during social interaction. In contrast, silencing CB⁺ neurons increased firing in a similar proportion of pSST⁺ neurons under baseline and social conditions (Supplementary Fig. 16h-j), indicating that CB+ neurons provide relatively stable inhibition of SST+ neurons. Together, these results demonstrate reciprocal inhibition between SST⁺ and CB⁺ neurons in vivo, and that this interaction may help stabilize social memory.

SST+-dLS neurons and CB+-vLS neurons preferentially receive stronger glutamatergic inputs from vCA1d and vCA1v pyramidal neurons

Having established the critical roles of SST+ and CB+ neurons in social memory acquisition, we next examined whether they have distinct synaptic connections. To obtain cell type-specific maps of synaptic inputs for both neurons, we utilized pseudotyped rabies virus (RV)-mediated trans-synaptic tracing to label monosynaptic inputs for SST+-dLS and CB+-vLS neurons (Fig. 5a; Supplementary Fig. 17a, b)64. The results showed that the majority of monosynaptic inputs to both SST+-dLS and CB+-vLS neurons were from hippocampal and hypothalamic regions (Supplementary Fig. 17a, b). Notably, vCA1 contained a particularly high density of RV-labeled neurons (Supplementary Fig. 17a, b), drawing our attention due to its established role in regulating social memory9. Interestingly, the RV-labeled vCA1 input neurons to SST+-dLS and vLS-CB+ neurons showed very different distribution patterns along the dorsal-ventral axis of vCA1, with SST+-dLS neurons receiving more inputs from the dorsal part of vCA1 (vCA1d) and CB+-vLS neurons receiving more inputs from the ventral parts of vCA1 (vCA1v) (Fig. 5b-d), consistent with the finding that the soma locations of CA1 pyramidal neurons correlate with their axon tip locations in the LS (See Figure 8D in ref65). We also reanalyzed previously published single-neuron projectomes of mouse hippocampus65 and found that dLS-projecting vCA1 neurons are preferentially localized in the vCA1d region (Supplementary Fig. 18a-c), while vLS-projecting vCA1 neurons are preferentially localized in the vCA1v region (Supplementary Fig. 18d-f). These findings confirm the correlation between vCA1 soma locations and the intensity of axonal projections in the LS.

Since CA2 is also known to regulate social memory, we next investigated whether SST+-dLS neurons receive monosynaptic inputs from CA2 neurons. To do this, we performed additional RV tracing experiments combined with immunostaining for RGS14, a molecular marker of CA2 neurons, (Supplementary Fig. 19). We found that 10.64% ± 1.39% of RGS14+ CA2 neurons were double-labeled with GFP, indicating that a subset projects to SST+-dLS neurons. However, these neurons represented only 3.12% ± 0.17% of the total GFP+ input population in the hippocampus, suggesting that CA2 provides a relatively minor input compared to vCA1. Based on these findings, we focused subsequent experiments on the vCA1→LS circuit.

To assay functional synaptic connections between vCA1 and LS neurons, we injected AAV-CaMKII-ChR2-EYFP into the vCA1 of C57 mice and performed patch-clamp recordings in LS neurons. Dense EYFP+ axonal fibers were visible in the LS (Supplementary Fig. 17c), suggesting potential synaptic connections between the vCA1 and LS. Based on voltage-clamp recordings, almost all neurons exhibited both excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) (measured with membrane potential at −70 mV) and IPSCs (measured at 0 mV) in response to laser stimulation (Supplementary Fig. 17d). TTX/4-AP reduced EPSC amplitude, but CNQX eliminated the EPSCs, confirming mediation by monosynaptic glutamatergic inputs (Supplementary Fig. 17d, e). However, TTX/4-AP completely blocked the IPSCs, suggesting mediation by disynaptic inhibition from local GABAergic neurons (Supplementary Fig. 17d, f).

To determine whether vCA1d and vCA1v neurons differentially innervate SST+ and CB+ neurons, we injected AAV-CaMKII-ChR2-EYFP into the vCA1d or vCA1v, together with AAV-fDIO-H2B-GFP and AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry into the dLS and vLS of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice (Fig. 5e). We then performed dual whole-cell recordings of SST+-dLS and CB+-vLS neurons labeled with GFP and mCherry, respectively (Fig. 5f), while laser stimulation was applied to activate synaptic inputs from vCA1d (Fig. 5f, g) or vCA1v (Fig. 5f, h). We found that laser stimulation of vCA1d inputs evoked stronger EPSCs in SST+-dLS neurons than in CB+-vLS neurons (Fig. 5g). Conversely, laser stimulation of vCA1v inputs evoked stronger EPSCs in CB+-vLS neurons than in SST+-dLS neurons (Fig. 5h). Both results suggest that vCA1d and vCA1v pyramidal neurons preferentially provide stronger synaptic inputs to SST+-dLS neurons and CB+-vLS neurons, respectively. This is consistent with the observed gradient distribution of RV-labled vCA1 input neurons to SST+-dLS and CB+-vLS neurons (Fig. 5b-d).

vCA1d→dLS and vCA1v→vLS pathways bidirectionally regulate social memory acquisition

To test the role of vCA1d and vCA1v, we first investigated whether the vCA1d→dLS pathways regulate social memory. We bilaterally injected AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-tdTomato into the dLS and AAV-DIO-EGFP-2A-TeNT into the vCA1d of C57 mice (Fig. 6a). TeNT silencing of dLS-projecting vCA1d neurons significantly reduced anxiety without affecting recognition (Supplementary Fig. 20b, c). Furthermore, inactivation of vCA1d→dLS pathway with TeNT impaired social memory at a 10-min interval (Fig. 6b) and blocked the enhanced theta oscillations during social interaction (Supplementary Fig. 20d), without altering baseline sociability (Supplementary Fig. 20a). Consistently, TeNT silencing of dLS-projecting vCA1d neurons also impaired social memory of the familiar mouse in the five-trial social memory assay (Fig. 6c), confirming the necessity of dLS-projecting vCA1d neurons for social memory.

Next, we explored whether vCA1d→dLS projections are essential for increased theta oscillations and social memory. To test this, we injected AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-EGFP and AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato into the dLS and vCA1d of C57 mice respectively, followed by optical fiber implantation above the dLS (Fig. 6d). To block this pathway, we delivered laser pulses to inhibit axonal terminals of vCA1d neurons in the dLS. This optogenetic silencing of vCA1d→dLS projections during memory acquisition blocked social memory at a 10-min interval, but did not affect baseline sociability (Fig. 6e; Supplementary Fig. 20f). In contrast, inhibiting the same projection during memory recall had no effect on social memory (Fig. 6f). To further explore the role of this pathway in theta activity, we injected AAV-CaMKII-eArchT3.0-EGFP into the vCA1d of C57 mice and implanted an LFP-recording optrode in the dLS (Supplementary Fig. 20e). Laser stimulation blocked the enhanced theta oscillations typically observed during social interaction (Supplementary Fig. 20e). These results suggest that vCA1d→dLS projections are necessary for both enhanced theta oscillations and social memory acquisition, consistent with the role of SST+-dLS neurons in regulating social memory acquisition.

We then examined whether the vCA1v→vLS pathways regulate social memory. We bilaterally injected AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-EGFP and AAV-DIO-hM3Dq-mCherry into the vLS and vCA1v of C57 mice, respectively (Fig. 6g). Chemogenetic activation of vLS-projecting vCA1v neurons reduced anxiety without changing recognition (Supplementary Fig. 20h, i). Additionally, activation of vLS-projecting vCA1v neurons impaired social memory at a 10-min interval, without altering baseline sociability (Fig. 6h; Supplementary Fig. 20g). In the five-trial social memory assay, activation of vLS-projecting vCA1v neurons impaired social memory of the familiar mouse in the first four trials (Fig. 6i).

To determine whether vCA1v→vLS projections regulate social memory, we injected AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-tdTomato and AAV-DIO-ChR2-EGFP into the vLS and vCA1v of C57 mice respectively, followed by optical fiber implantation above the vLS (Fig. 6j). Optogenetic activation of vCA1v→vLS projections during memory acquisition blocked social memory at a 10-min interval (Fig. 6k), whereas activation of these projections during memory recall did not affect social memory (Fig. 6l). These findings suggest that vCA1v→vLS projections inhibit social memory acquisition, correlating with the finding that activation of CB+-vLS neurons suppresses social memory acquisition.

Previous studies have shown that vCA1 region projects to both LS and NAc, including neurons that project exclusively to LS, exclusively to NAc, and a small subset that project to both regions21. To quantify the proportion of dual-projecting neurons, we performed retrograde tracing by injecting CTB-555 into the NAc and CTB-488 into the vLS, and analyzed labeled neurons in the vCA1. We found that 10.95% ± 1.19% of LS-projecting vCA1 neurons (green) also projected to the NAc, and 15.82% ± 1.24% of NAc-projecting vCA1 neurons (red) also projected to the LS (Supplementary Fig. 21a-d), suggesting that dual-projecting neurons comprise only a small fraction of the vCA1 neurons. Notably, global silencing of vCA1 neurons disrupts both social memory recall and acquisition (see Figure S8 in ref9), whereas selective inhibition of vCA1→NAc projections impairs recall alone9. Together with these findings, our data support a model in which vCA1→LS and vCA1→NAc pathways contribute to different phases of social memory: the vCA1→LS projection primarily supports memory acquisition, whereas the vCA1→NAc pathway is more important for memory recall.

To examine the function of vCA1 neurons that project specifically to the NAc, we bilaterally injected AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-EGFP and AAV-Cre-off-eNpHR3.0-mCherry into the LS and vCA1 of C57 mice, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 21e), thereby restricting expression of eNpHR3.0 to vCA1 neurons that do not project to the LS. Optogenetic silencing of these non-LS projecting vCA1 neurons during memory acquisition did not affect social memory at a 10-min interval (Supplementary Fig. 21f), but silencing of these neurons during memory recall abolished social memory (Supplementary Fig. 21g). Similarly, inhibition of non-LS-projecting vCA1→NAc terminals selectively impaired memory recall without affecting acquisition (Supplementary Fig. 21h-j).

Collectively, these findings support a model in which vCA1→LS and vCA1→NAc projections form two parallel and functionally distinct circuits that regulate social memory acquisition and recall, respectively. Furthermore, within the vCA1→LS circuit, the vCA1d→dLS and vCA1v→vLS pathways appear to exert contrasting influences on social memory acquisition.

Presynaptic plasticity at vCA1d→dLS excitatory synapses to SST+ neurons

The above findings suggest that during social memory acquisition, vCA1d excitatory inputs may specifically regulate SST+-dLS neurons, whereas vCA1v excitatory inputs may specifically regulate CB+-vLS neurons. Therefore, we asked whether social memory acquisition affects synaptic strength at vCA1-LS excitatory synapses. To address this, we recorded spontaneous EPSCs (sEPSCs) in SST+-dLS and CB+-vLS neurons. To label SST+ or CB+ neurons, AAV-CAG-DIO-H2B-mCherry was injected into the dLS of SST-Cre or vLS of CB-Cre mice. Two weeks later, we subjected the mice to social memory acquisition paradigm (Fig. 7a, also see Methods) and prepared LS slices for sEPSC recordings. Interestingly, we found a significant increase in the frequency of sEPSCs in SST+-dLS neurons following social interaction compared to control mice (Fig. 7b-d), whereas sEPSCs in CB+-vLS neurons remained unchanged (Fig. 7e-g). To exclude potential confounds from motor activity, we recorded sEPSCs from SST+-dLS neurons in mice exposed to either a rotating (Running) or stationary (Control) rotarod (Supplementary Fig. 22a). No differences were observed in sEPSC frequency or amplitude between groups (Supplementary Fig. 22b-d), indicating that locomotion alone does not account for the synaptic changes. The social interaction-induced increase in sEPSC frequency in SST+-dLS neurons suggests an enhancement in either presynaptic release probability (Pr) or synapse number. To distinguish between these two probabilities, we measured the paired-pulse ratios (PPRs) of vCA1-LS EPSCs (Fig. 7h), as PPR is inversely related to Pr66. We observed a significant reduction in the PPRs of vCA1d→dLS EPSCs in SST+ neurons (Fig. 7i), but no change in the PPR of vCA1v→vLS EPSCs in CB+ neurons (Fig. 7j), suggesting that social interaction increased the Pr specifically at vCA1d→SST+-dLS synapses. Taken together, these results suggest that vCA1d excitatory synapses to SST+-dLS neurons undergo synaptic potentiation during social memory acquisition.

SST+-dLS→LHA and CB+-vLS→AHN pathways enhance and suppress social memory acquisition

Having demonstrated that SST+ and CB+ neurons exert bidirectional control over social memory, we next asked whether these divergent effects are mediated by distinct downstream projections. To map efferent pathways, we performed anterograde tracing by injecting AAV-DIO-EGFP into the LS of SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice (Supplementary Fig. 23a, b). Both SST+ and CB+ neurons project to multiple downstream targets, including BNST, NAc, and several hypothalamic subregions such as the preoptic area (POA), AHN, LHA, supramammillary nucleus (SUM), and posterior hypothalamic nucleus (PH)—regions known to contribute to diverse social behaviors67-69. Notably, SST+-dLS neurons sent more projections to the LHA, while CB+-vLS neurons projected comparably to both the AHN and LHA (Supplementary Fig. 23c, d). Moreover, the AHN contained a higher density of Gad1⁺ GABAergic neurons compared to Slc17a6⁺ glutamatergic neurons, while the LHA displayed the opposite pattern, with a greater density of Slc17a6⁺ glutamatergic neurons (Supplementary Fig. 25).

To determine whether above circuits are required for social memory, we injected AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato into the dLS of SST-Cre mice, followed by optical fiber implantation above the ArchT-expressing axonal terminals in the AHN (Fig. 8a), LHA (Fig. 8d), and POA (Supplementary Fig. 23e). ArchT silencing of the SST+-dLS→AHN or SST+-dLS→POA pathways during the memory acquisition phase did not affect social memory (Fig. 8c; Supplementary Fig. 23g). In contrast, silencing the SST+-dLS→LHA pathway during memory acquisition blocked social memory without affecting novel object preference (Fig. 8f; Supplementary Fig. 24g). ArchT silencing of all three pathways did not change baseline sociability (Fig. 8b, e; Supplementary Fig. 23f). Moreover, silencing the SST+-dLS→LHA pathway significantly reduced anxiety levels (Supplementary Fig. 24e, f). To validate the SST+-dLS→LHA pathway, we injected AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP into the dLS of SST-Cre mice and performed slice physiology (Supplementary Fig. 24a, b). In acute LHA slices, we detected light-evoked IPSCs in 15 out of 17 LHA neurons, which were completely abrogated by PTX (Supplementary Fig. 24c, d), confirming that SST+-dLS neurons formed functional GABAergic synapses with LHA neurons. Together, these results show that GABAergic projections from SST+-dLS neurons to LHA neurons are necessary for social memory.

Considering the opposite effect of the SST+ and CB+ neurons on social memory, we next examined whether activation of vLS-CB+ circuits can impair social memory. AAV-DIO- ChR2-EYFP was injected into the vLS of CB-Cre mice, followed by optical fiber implantation above the ChR2+ axonal terminals in the AHN (Fig. 8g), LHA (Fig. 8j), and POA (Supplementary Fig. 23h), respectively. Light stimulation of the CB+-vLS→LHA or CB+-vLS→POA pathways had no effect on social memory or baseline sociability (Fig. 8k, l; Supplementary Fig. 23i, j). In contrast, activation of the CB+-vLS→AHN pathway during memory acquisition blocked social memory without altering baseline sociability (Fig. 8h, i). Moreover, activation of the CB+-vLS→AHN pathway did not change anxiety levels or the preference for the novel object (Supplementary Fig. 24l-n). To validate the CB+-vLS→AHN pathway, we injected AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP into the vLS of CB-Cre mice and performed slice physiology (Supplementary Fig. 24h, i). In acute AHN slices, we observed light-evoked IPSCs in 19 out of 20 AHN neurons, which were eliminated by PTX (Supplementary Fig. 24j, k), confirming functional GABAergic connections between CB+-vLS neurons and AHN neurons. Together, these findings demonstrate that the CB+-vLS→AHN pathway suppresses social memory.
paper_content.methods:
Animals. All experimental procedures were performed following protocols approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Huazhong University of Science and Technology, China. The SST-ires-Cre (SST-Cre), SST-ires-Flp (SST-Flp), CB-ires-Cre (CB-Cre), Rosa26-LSL-tdTomato (Ai14), Esr1-2a-Cre (Esr1-Cre) and Rosa26-LSL-H2B-GFP (LSL-H2B-GFP) mouse lines were imported from the Jackson Laboratory (SST-Cre: #013044; SST-Flp: #028579; CB-Cre: #028532; Ai14: #007914; Esr1-Cre: #0017913; LSL-H2B-GFP: #036761; JAX Mice and Services, USA). The C57BL/6 mice were purchased from the Animal Center of Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Mice (3–5 per cage) were housed under a 12-h light/dark cycle at an ambient temperature of 20–24 °C and relative humidity of 30–70%, with food and water provided ad libitum. We have only used male mice in this study because the social behaviors of laboratory mice exhibit sex- and strain-dependent behavioral parameters90,91.

Single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq)

Tissue collection and snRNA-seq. Single nuclei were isolated as described previously92. The LS was micro-dissected from six male C57BL/6 mice (2-month-old). Coronal LS sections (300-μm thick) spanning bregma +1.10 mm to −0.10 mm (Allen Brain Atlas, atlas.brain-map.org) were prepared with a vibratome, and four consecutive slices were collected. To minimize contamination from adjacent regions (e.g., MS, NAc, striatum, and corpus callosum), LS tissue was carefully isolated under a dissection microscope using a fine angled knife (#10056-12, FST) and fine forceps. Surrounding brain regions were removed, leaving only the LS (highlighted in purple in Supplementary Fig. 1a) for analysis. Tissues were rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until processing.

For single-nuclear suspension, tissues were thawed and homogenized in homogenization buffer containing 250 mM sucrose, 25 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl , 10 mM Tris, 0.1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), mini protease 2 inhibitor cocktail (#11836153001; Roche, Switzerland), 0.4 U/μL RNase inhibitor, 1% BSA, and 0.1% NP40. Samples were centrifuged (500 g, 5 min, 4 ℃), washed with homogenization buffer, and repetitively pipetted to generate a nuclear suspension. The nuclear suspensions were again centrifuged (500 g, 5 min, 4 ℃) and resuspended in cold 1 × phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). After nucleus counting, the DNBSEQTM technology platform (BGI Genomics, China) and DNBelab C4 Single-Cell Library Prep Set (#1000021082; MGI, China) were used for snRNA-seq library preparation93. Briefly, the single-nucleus suspensions were converted to barcoded libraries using droplet generation, emulsion breakage, bead collection, reverse transcription, cDNA amplification, and purification. Indexed sequencing libraries were constructed according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Sequencing library quality was evaluated using a QubitTM ssDNA Assay Kit (#Q10212; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Libraries were sequenced using an ultra-high-throughput DIPSEQ T1 sequencer with the following strategy: 30 bp for read 1, inclusive of 10 bp cell barcode 1, 10 bp cell barcode 2, and 10 bp unique molecular identifier (UMI), 100 bp of transcript sequence for read 2, and 10 bp for sample index.

SnRNA-seq data processing. Raw sequencing reads were filtered and demultiplexed using PISA (https://github.com/shiquan/PISA)94. Reads were aligned to the GRCm38 mouse genome using STAR (v2.7.4a) and sorted by Sambamba (v0.7.0).

Cell clustering and cell type identification. Cell clustering was performed using the Seurat (v4.1.0) R toolkit (https://github.com/satijalab/seurat). Qualified cells were filtered according to number of detected genes (between 500 and 6 500) and percentage of mitochondrial genes (< 0.1%). Genes expressed in < 3 cells were removed. The filtered dataset was log-normalized and scaled, and principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted. The first 18 PCs were used for graph-based clustering in Seurat using the Louvain algorithm. Non-neuronal clusters were identified by expression of Pdgfra, Oligo1, Mki67, Slc1a3, Mal, C1qa, Foxj1, and Cldn5 (Supplementary Fig. 1). A cluster with high mitochondrial gene expression and low detected genes was removed (data not shown). The remaining neuronal cells were then reclustered and processed using the same pipeline. Clusters were designated “non-LS” only if they expressed more than ten well-established markers for neighboring regions (e.g., MS, NAc) (Supplementary Fig. 2). Corresponding in-situ hybridization (ISH) images were adapted from Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, mouse.brain-map.org, and details are provided in Supplementary Table 3. Analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in all neuronal clusters was performed using the FindAllMarkers function in Seurat. Fold-changes and p-values of gene expression between Sst+ and Calb1+ clusters were calculated using the FindMarkers function with the MAST algorithm95.

Immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis. Mice were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane, then perfused with PBS followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Brains were dissected and post-fixed in 4% PFA for 6 h at 4 °C, then immersed in 30% sucrose for 2 days before sectioning (30 μm) on a cryostat (Leica CM1050; Leica Biosystems, Germany). For IHC, slices were pre-incubated in blocking solution (10% normal goat serum with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) for 1 h at room temperature (RT) and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, including rabbit anti-CB (1:500, #14479-1-AP; Proteintech, China), mouse anti-NeuN (1:1 000, #MAB377; Merck, Germany), guinea pig anti-c-fos (1:1 000, #226004; SYSY, Germany), rabbit anti-RGS14 (1:1 000, #16258-1-AP; Proteintech, China), rat anti-mCherry (1:1 000, #M11217; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), and rabbit anti-GFP (1:1 000, #A-11122; Thermo Fisher Scientific). The slices were washed in PBS (10 min, three times) and incubated with secondary antibodies (1:1 000, goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 488, goat anti-rat Alexa Fluor 546, goat anti-guinea pig Alexa Fluor 633, and goat anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 647; Invitrogen, USA) for 2 h at RT. Next, the slices were mounted on positive-charged glass slides, coverslipped, and imaged using a confocal microscope (LSM 780, Carl Zeiss, Germany). The images were analyzed using Fiji ImageJ v1.52n.

c-fos labeling. Two-month-old male SST-Cre/Ai14 mice were singly housed in clean cages for 7 days before the experiment, then randomly divided into test and control groups. A test mouse was placed into a clean cage with a novel juvenile mouse. A control mouse was placed into an empty cage. After 10 min, mice from both groups were returned to their home cages for 1.5 h, then perfused with 4% PFA for IHC analysis (as above). All unbiased analyses were done manually from blinded groups.

Single-molecule fluorescent in-situ hybridization (smFISH). Two-month-old male mice were used for all experiments. Hybridization chain reaction (HCR) was used to detect mRNA expressions of Sst, Gad1 and Slc17a696. We designed probes targeting the coding and 3′UTR regions of Sst, Gad1 and Slc17a6 (Sangon Biotech, China). All solutions used for hybridization were prepared using RNase-free reagents and diethylpyrocarbonate (DEPC)-treated double deionized water (ddH O). After perfusion, brains were post-fixed in 4% PFA for 24 h, dehydrated in 20%–30% DEPC-treated sucrose for 24 h, cryosectioned (30 μm), and mounted onto SuperFrost glass slides. The sections were then immersed in 70% ethanol for 16 h at 4 °C, permeabilized by 0.5% Triton X-100 for 1 h at 37 °C, and treated with 10 µg/mL protease K to improve mRNA accessibility. After twice washing in 1 × PBS at RT, the brain sections were pre-hybridized in probe hybridization buffer for 10 min at 37 °C and further incubated with HCR probe (10 µM, Supplementary Table 1) at 37 °C for 3 h. After mRNA hybridization, washing and amplification procedures were conducted as described previously96.

RNAscope-FISH. Tissue preparation for RNAscope-FISH followed the same protocol as smFISH. Brains were cryosectioned into 20-μm sections and mounted onto SuperFrost glass slides. RNAscope-FISH was performed using the RNAscope v2 Assay kit (cat. #323100, Advanced Cell Diagnostics, USA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The following target probes were used: Sst (cat. #404631-C1), Calb1 (cat. #428431-C2), Nts (cat. #420441-C3), Prlr (cat. #430791-C3), Htr2c (cat. #401001-C3), and Glp1r (cat. #418851-C2). All probes were obtained from Advanced Cell Diagnostics (ACDBio, USA).

Virus preparation. Two AAV serotypes (AAV2/9 and AAV2-retro) were used. AAV2-retro was used to retrogradely label projection neurons in the vCA197. The plasmid for AAV-DIO-EGFP-2A-TeNT was a gift from Dr. Thomas C. Südhof (Stanford University). All AAVs (AAV-DIO-EGFP, AAV-DIO-tdTomato, AAV-DIO-mCherry, AAV-fDIO-H2B-mCherry, AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry, AAV-DIO-EGFP-2A-TeNT, AAV-DIO-hM3Dq-mCherry, AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato, AAV-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV-fDIO-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV-CaMKII-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV-Syn-Cre-off-eNpHR3.0-mCherry, AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-EGFP, AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-tdTomato, AAV-CaMKll-eArchT3.0-EGFP, AAV-Syn-DIO-TVA-2a-RG-2a-mCherry), and the SAD ΔG-GFP pseudotyped rabies virus were purchased from Shanghai Taitool Bioscience (China) or Brain Case (China). The final viral vector titers of AAVs ranged from 3 to 8 × 1012 particles/mL. The final titer of the SAD ΔG-GFP pseudotyped rabies virus was 108 infecting units/mL.

Stereotaxic injection. Mice were anesthetized with tribromoethanol (150–250 mg/kg, i.p.). Standard surgery was performed to expose the brain surface above the LS or ventral hippocampus. Coordinates for the LS injections in SST-Cre were: bregma 0.86 mm, lateral ±0.35 mm, and dura −2.5 mm. Coordinates for the LS injections in CB-Cre were: bregma 0.5 mm, lateral ±0.37 mm, and dura −3.0 mm. Coordinates for hippocampal vCA1d injection were: bregma −3.28 mm, lateral ±3.10 mm, dura −1.4 mm. Coordinates for hippocampal vCA1v injection were: bregma −3.28 mm, lateral ±3.10 mm, dura −3.4 mm. AAVs (200–400 nL) were stereotaxically injected using a glass pipette connected to a Nanoliter Injector MICRO-2T (World Precision Instruments, Inc., USA) at a slow flow rate of 0.12 μL/min. The pipette was withdrawn at least 10 min after the viral injection. AAV-DIO-EGFP, AAV-DIOS-tdTomato, or AAV-DIO-mCherry were bilaterally injected into the LS of SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice for control experiments. Experimental designs related to viral injection are summarized in Supplementary Table 2. Schematics of injection sites in the main and supplementary figures were adapted from reference brain images from Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, atlas.brain-map.org.

Optical fiber implantation. Three weeks after AAV injection, ceramic ferrules with an optical fiber (200-μm diameter, N.A. 0.37, Inper Inc., China) were bilaterally implanted with the fiber tips on the top of the dLS (bregma 0.86 mm, lateral ±1.10 mm, and dura −2.55 mm) at a 14° angle and the vLS (bregma 0.5 mm, lateral ±1.47 mm, and dura −3.0 mm) at a 14° angle, the vCA1 (bregma−3.28 mm, lateral ± 3.5 mm, and dura −2.65 mm), the NAc (bregma 1.42 mm, lateral ± 1.07 mm, and dura −3.46 mm) at a 8° angle, the POA (bregma −0.10 mm, lateral ± 1.3 mm, and dura −4.6 mm) at a 10° angle, the AHN (bregma −0.82 mm, lateral ± 1.25 mm, and dura −4.5 mm) at a 8° angle, and the LHA (bregma −2.06 mm, lateral ± 1.0 mm, and dura −5.0 mm). The ferrules were secured onto the skull with dental cement. Optogenetic experiments were performed at least 6 weeks after AAV injection. The tip of the optical fiber was usually located 100~500 μm above the AAV injection center. Only mice with a correct injection sites and optical fiber tracks above the target regions were included in the analyses. Animals with off-target injections or misplaced fibers were excluded, and the number of exclusions is reported in Supplementary Table 4. In very rare cases, control mice with abnormal brain structures (e.g., cerebral edema) were also excluded.

Optogenetic manipulation. The optical fiber cable was connected via patch cords and 1 × 2 Fiber-optic Rotary Joints (Doric Lenses, Canada) to a laser (Shanghai Dream Lasers Technology, China). For ChR2 activation, blue laser pulses (473 nm, 5, 10, or 20 Hz, 5 ms/pulse) were applied during certain behavioral stages. For ArchT silencing, a continuous green laser (532 nm) was applied. Laser power at the optical fiber tip was measured with a power meter (PM100D, Thorlabs, USA) and calibrated to 10 mW/mm2.

Chemogenetic manipulation. For chemogenetic manipulation of LS CB+ neurons, CB-Cre mice were injected with AAV-DIO-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry or AAV-DIO-mCherry (Control). Clozapine-N-oxide (CNO, 5 mg/kg dissolved in saline; #4936, Tocris Bioscience, UK) or saline was i.p. injected 30 min prior to behavioral tests.

Mouse behaviors

Preparation for behavioral tests. Behavioral tests were performed at least 3 weeks after AAV injection. All animals were handled daily for 3 days in advance and habituated for 3 h in the test room before behavioral tests. All apparatuses were cleaned with 75% ethanol to eliminate odors. All behavioral tests were conducted in the light phase (10:00–19:00). All experiments were video-recorded and analyzed using a tracking system (Biobserve, Germany).

Open field test (OFT). White-colored plastic boxes (40 × 40 × 40 cm) were used as the open field chambers. Mice were individually placed into the center of the box and allowed to freely explore for 10 min. Total distance travelled, time spent in center arena (20 × 20 cm), distance travelled in center, and number of visits to center were analyzed.

Elevated plus maze (EPM). The maze consisted of two open arms (35 × 6 cm), two closed arms (35 × 6 × 15 cm), and a central connecting region (6 × 6 cm), positioned 45 cm above the ground. Mice were individually placed in the central region with their head facing the open arm and allowed to freely explore for 5 min. Time spent and number of entries in the open arms vs. closed arms were recorded.

Novel object recognition test-1 (NORT-1). NORT was conducted to evaluate non-social recognition ability, as previously described98. For the training phase, two identical objects (blue cylindrical glass bottles) were symmetrically placed in the open field chamber. Each mouse was allowed to freely explore the objects for 10 min, then returned to its home cage. After 1 h, a novel object (gray cubic brick) was used to randomly replace one of the familiar objects. The test mouse was returned to the chamber and time spent interacting with the objects was recorded. We cumulatively counted the first 20 s that the mouse interacted with the two objects. The discrimination index was calculated by: (T – T ) / (T + T ), where T and T represent time spent exploring novel and familiar objects, respectively.

Novel object recognition test-2 (NORT-2). This test was adapted as previously described15. For the habituation phase, the subject mouse was introduced into the open field chamber for 5 min. Then two identical objects (blue cylindrical glass bottles) were symmetrically placed in opposite corners of the open field chamber. Each mouse was allowed to freely explore the objects for 10 min (learning phase), then returned to its home cage. After 30 min, a novel object (gray cubic brick) was used to randomly replace one of the familiar objects. The test mouse was returned to the chamber and were allowed to explore for 5 minutes. The discrimination index was calculated by: (T – T ) / (T + T ), where T and T represent time spent exploring novel and familiar objects, respectively, during the 5-min period.

Three-chamber social test. The classical three-chamber social test was performed as previously described2. The apparatus was divided into three chambers (30 × 30 × 30 cm), with connecting doors. Two cylinders (5-cm circular base radius and 15-cm height) were placed in the middle of the side chambers. The behavioral test consisted of three sessions, including habituation (10 min), sociability test (10 min), and social memory test (10 min). During habituation, the test mouse was allowed to freely explore the arena for 10 min. For the familiarization session, a novel stranger mouse (age and sex matched, stranger 1) was randomly placed in the left or right cylinder, with the other cylinder empty. The subject mouse was allowed to explore the two cylinders (with or without stranger 1) for 10 min. Interaction time was defined as the time in which the subject mouse spent investigating each cylinder (snout within 2 cm of the mesh barrier), as described previously2. The social index was calculated by: social index = (T – T ) / (T + T ), where T and T represent interaction time for the two cylinders, respectively. For the social memory test session, a novel stranger mouse (stranger 2) was randomly placed in the left or right cylinder, and the now familiar mouse (stranger 1) was placed in the other cylinder. The test mouse was allowed to explore the two cylinders (with novel or familiar stranger) for 10 min. Interaction time towards the familiar mouse (S1) and novel mouse (S2) was recorded. The social discrimination (SD) index was calculated by: SDI = (T – T ) / (T + T ). For most experiments, there was no interval between the familiarization and social memory test sessions. For the prolonged social memory test, the social memory session was performed after an interval of 10–60 min (Supplementary Fig. 11g) or 40 min (Fig. 2l and 4f).

For the social memory experiments related to vCA1 (Fig. 6; Supplementary Fig. 21), a novel stranger mouse (age- and sex-matched, stranger 1) and a novel object (blue brick, 4 × 4 × 6 cm) were randomly placed in the left or right cylinder during the familiarization session. The social memory test session was carried out after an interval of 10 min.

For the two-round social memory test (Supplementary Fig 12), we introduced a 10‑min interval between the first social memory recall (S1 vs. S2) and the subsequent social memory acquisition (S3).

5-trial social memory assay. This test was performed as previously described 2,15. The test mouse was placed in a clean cage for a 4-h habituation period. Subsequently, a novel mouse (5-6 weeks old) was introduced into the cage for four consecutive 1-min trials with a 10-min inter-trial interval. On the fifth trial, a second novel stimulus animal was presented. The direct interaction time was analyzed frame by frame from the video using a Matlab code as previously described53.

Real-time conditioned place preference (RT-CPP). The RT-CPP apparatus consisted of two adjacent chambers (20 × 30 × 30 cm), which were visually (black and white) and tactilely (smooth and rough) different. One chamber was randomly assigned as the initial photostimulated side (phase 1). After 10 min, the stimulated side was switched to the previously non-stimulated chamber (phase 2). In each session, a mouse with optical fibers was placed into the non-photostimulated side and allowed to freely explore the two side chambers. Each time the mouse entered the photostimulated side, green (532 nm) light was delivered until the mouse returned to the non-photostimulated side. There was no interruption between phase 1 and phase 2. Time spent in each chamber (stimulated vs. non-stimulated) was recorded, and preference for the photostimulated side was calculated by: preference = percentage of time spent in photostimulated side – percentage of time spent in non-photostimulated side.

Pseudotyped rabies virus-mediated retrograde tracing and AAV-mediated anterograde tracing. For retrograde tracing, we first unilaterally injected 80 nL of AAV-Syn-DIO-TVA-2a-RG-2a-mCherry into the dLS of SST-Cre or the vLS of CB-Cre mice, respectively. Three weeks later, 300 nL of RV-ΔG-GFP (glycoprotein deficient, GFP-expressing rabies virus) was injected into the same location under biosafety level 2 conditions as above. One week after RV -ΔG-GFP injection, mice were euthanized and their brains were collected. For anterograde tracing, AAV-DIO-EGFP (50 nL) were unilaterally injected into the dLS of SST-Cre or the vLS of CB-Cre mice, respectively. Coronal slices (40 μm) were cryosectioned as above, and every third section was collected for imaging analysis. Fluorescence images were acquired with a SV120 Olympus automatic slide scanner (10× objective, 0.4 NA, Japan).

To quantify rabies virus (RV) labeled neurons along the dorsal-to-ventral axis of vCA1, we adapted a previously described method99. Briefly, A spline curve was first drawn along the vCA1 pyramidal layer from its dorsal to ventral end and divided into 100 equal segments. RV-labeled neurons were then counted within each segment. Vertical boundaries for each segment were defined by the tangent to the spline at the corresponding point. In Fig. 5d, the X-axis (0–100) represents the relative position along the vCA1 dorsal–ventral axis, where 0 denotes the most dorsal region and 100 the most ventral region.

In-vivo electrophysiology

In-vivo single-unit recordings and data analysis. In-vivo electrophysiological recordings were performed in freely moving or head-fixed mice as per previous study53,59. Opto-electrodes (optrodes) consisted of a custom-designed miniature micro-drive containing 16 movable electrodes (25.4-μm nickel-chromium wire, #761500; A-M System, USA) and an optical fiber in the center. Final resistance of the electrodes was 700–800 kΩ. AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato was bilaterally injected into the LS of 7–8-week-old SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice. Three weeks later, mice were anesthetized with tribromoethanol (150–250 mg/kg, i.p.) and placed in a stereotaxic frame. The mice were properly aligned and the optrodes were implanted into the LS. Dental cement was applied to fully cover the exposed skull and secure the implants. After surgery, mice were returned to their home cage and allowed to recover for at least 10 days before recording.

To record single-unit activity in freely moving mice (Supplementary Fig. 9b), we recorded neuronal activity during social interactions100. First, the experimental mouse was placed in the test arena (40 × 40 × 40 cm) for 5 min to record baseline activity. A novel stranger mouse was then introduced to the chamber. Both mice were separated by a plastic wall with small holes (7.5 mm) (Fig. 3b; Supplementary Fig. 9b), which allowed social interaction with each other. Neuronal activity was recorded for another 5 or 20 min during social interaction. Wide-band (WB) signals were recorded for offline sorting and mouse behaviors were videotaped simultaneously for further analysis.

To record single-unit activity in head-fixed mice (Supplementary Fig. 9j-m), we used a previously established recording setup53, in which mice were head-fixed using a 3D-printed head ring and allowed to run freely on a wheel. Each mouse was presented with either an anesthetized stranger mouse (male, 5-6 weeks old) or a novel object (3 × 3 × 3 cm) placed on a movable platform. Once positioned, the stimulus was approximately 0.5 cm from the nose of the recording mouse. For SST+ neuron recordings during social interactions, the stimulus was presented for 5 s with 25 s intervals, repeated for 20 trials.

To record mutual inhibition during social interactions in vivo (Supplementary Fig. 16), neuronal activity was recorded during a 10-min baseline period or a 10-min social interaction period, during which an anesthetized male mouse was continuously presented. Optogenetic stimulation (λ = 532 nm, 3 s pulses, 10 s inter-pulse interval, 20 trials) was delivered within 1 minute of each recording condition.

Single-unit sorting was performed manually by Offline Sorter v4.0 (Plexon, Inc., USA). Spiking activities were digitized at 40 kHz and stored for offline sorting. The WB signals were high-pass filtered at 250 Hz and waveform detection thresholds were placed at -4.0 to -4.5 times the standard error of digital signal range, depending on the signal-noise ratio. The detected waveforms were aligned at the valley point, and two-dimensional principal component analysis (PCA) was used for separation of single-unit spikes. The distribution of inter-spike intervals (ISIs) from all isolated single-unit spikes exhibited recognizable refractory periods (> 1 ms). Only well-isolated units (L ratio < 0.2, isolation distance > 15) were included for analyses.

In-vivo firing rate analysis. Single-unit responses were analyzed using NeuroExplorer v5.0 (Plexon, Inc.). Well-separated single-unit spikes were collected to analyze neuronal responses to social stimuli. During 20-min social interactions, the start and end time points of each social bout were manually labeled by examining behavioral videos frame by frame. The ISIs of single-unit spikes during baseline and social interaction were compared to evaluate significant firing rate differences (p < 0.05, two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test). The mean and SD during the total recorded time were used for calculating firing rate Z-score. Neurons were considered as activated with a firing rate Z-score value > 2.0 during the 3 s of stimulus presentation101.

In-vivo cell type identification. To identify SST+ and CB+ single units, we utilized ArchT-mediated optic tagging102, whereby laser pulses (λ = 532 nm, 3 s long) were delivered via the optical fiber after each behavioral recording session (Supplementary Fig. 9).

In-vivo local field potential recording. Optrodes containing two-channel single electrodes (75-μm stainless steel wire, #793400; A-M System, USA) and an optical fiber were hand-made as described previously59. Local field potentials (LFPs) were sampled at 1 kHz with a low-pass filter at 250 Hz. The LFP power spectra across four frequency bands, including alpha (1–3 Hz), theta (4–12 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), and gamma (31–80 Hz), were analyzed. Power spectrum density (PSD) was calculated using NeuroExplorer v5.0 (Plexon Inc.). For optogenetic manipulation during LFP recordings, 5-ms blue light pulses (5, 10, and 20 Hz, λ = 473 nm) were used to activate SST+ neurons, whereas continuous green light (λ = 532 nm) was delivered to inhibit SST+ neurons or the vCA1d→dLS pathway.

In-vivo phase locking analysis. Single units and LFP recorded by the 16-channel optrode were used for phase-lock analysis to evaluate the relationship between theta oscillations and timestamps in SST+ and CB+ neurons in the LS, as described previously58,59. The oscillatory activity phase was extracted using Hilvert’s transformation and converted into angle degrees. Rayleigh test was used for circular uniformity to identify significant correlations between the timing of spikes and specific phase of the theta cycle58,59.

Slice electrophysiology and optogenetics. Mice were euthanized with isoflurane and coronal LS, AHN, or LHA slices (300-μm thick) were sectioned with a vibratome (VT1200S; Leica Biosystems, Germany) in cutting solution containing (in mM): 228 sucrose, 2.5 KCI, 26 NaHCO , 1 NaH PO ·2H O, 11 D-Glucose, 0.5 CaCl , and 7 MgCl , then transferred to artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) containing (in mM): 119 NaCl, 2.5 KCI, 26 NaHCO , 1 NaH PO ·2H O, 11 D-Glucose, 2.5 CaCl , and 1.3 MgCl (pH = 7.4). Slices were incubated at 35 °C for 30 min and then at RT until use. Recordings were performed in a submerged-style chamber mounted under an infrared-differential interference contrast (IR-DIC) microscope (BX-51 WI; Olympus, Japan). Whole-cell recordings were performed using a MultiClamp 700B amplifier and Digidata 1550B4 (Molecular Devices, USA). Patch pipette resistance was 4–6 MΩ. Signals were sampled at 20 kHz, filtered at 10 kHz, and analyzed using Clampex v10.4 (Molecular Devices).

To analyze electrophysiological properties, SST+ and CB+ neurons were visualized by tdTomato expression in SST-Cre/Ai14 or CB-Cre/Ai14 mice, respectively. TdTomato+ neurons were recorded with a K-gluconate-based internal solution containing (in mM): 135 K-gluconate, 10 HEPES, 8 KCl, 0.25 EGTA, 0.3 Na GTP, 2 MgATP, 7 phospho-creatine, and 0.1 spermine (pH 7.25–7.3; osmolarity 294–298). To compare the neuronal excitability, the recorded neurons were subjected to step current injections with different amplitudes ranging from 20 to 160 pA, and the number of action potentials (APs) was counted accordingly. To record HCN-mediated sag amplitudes, the recorded neurons were subjected to step current injections with different amplitudes ranging from –80 pA to –20 pA, and the sag amplitudes were estimated by subtracting the values at the onset of hyperpolarizing voltages (peak amplitude) from those at the end (steady-state) as previously described52.

For recording IPSCs from SST+ neurons, AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP was bilaterally injected into the LS of SST-Cre/Ai14 mice at postnatal day 35–40 (P35–P40). After 6 weeks, tdTomato-/EYFP- neurons (presumably Cre- neurons) in the LS were recorded using a KCl-based internal solution containing (in mM): 71 KCl, 72 K-gluconate, 10 HEPES, 2 MgCl , 0.025 BAPTA, and 2 MgATP (pH 7.25–7.3; osmolarity 295–300). To study inhibitory synapses from CB+ to SST+ neurons, AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP and AAV-fDIO-H2B-mCherry were bilaterally injected into the LS of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice at P35–P40. After 6 weeks, mCherry+ neurons (SST+ neurons) in the LS were recorded with the same KCl-based internal solution. Light (2 ms)-evoked IPSCs were recorded in the presence of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 50 μM; #0940, Tocris) and tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 μM; #1078, Tocris). D-(-)-2-amino-5-phosphonopentanoic acid (D-AP5, 50 μM; #0106, Tocris) and 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione disodium (CNQX, 20 μM; #1045, Tocris) or picrotoxin (PTX, 50 μM; #1128, Tocris) were perfused with ACSF to examine the neurotransmitter type used by ChR2-EYFP-expressing neurons. The inhibitory synapses from SST+ to CB+ neurons were also studied by injecting AAV-fDIO-ChR2-EYFP and AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry into the LS of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice. The SST+-dLS→LHA and CB+-vLS→AHN pathways were also validated as mentioned above.

For dual patch-clamp recordings, AAV-CaMKII-ChR2-EYFP was bilaterally injected into the vCA1d or vCA1v of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice at P35–P40. After 6 weeks, SST+ neurons in the dLS and CB+ neurons in the vLS were recorded using the K-gluconate-based internal solution. Light-induced excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) were recorded in SST+ and CB+ neurons simultaneously.

For sEPSC recordings, AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry was bilaterally injected into the LS of SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice at P45–P50. After two weeks, SST+ neurons in the dLS and CB+ neurons in the vLS were recorded using a CsMeSO -based internal solution (in mM): 140 CsMeSO , 10 HEPES, 8 CsCl, 0.25 EGTA, 0.3 Na GTP, 2 MgATP, 7 phospho-creatine, and 0.1 spermine (pH 7.25–7.3; osmolarity 295–300). The sEPSCs were recorded with 50 μM PTX in ACSF.

For recording the PPRs of vCA1-LS EPSCs, AAV-CaMKII-ChR2-EYFP and AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry were bilaterally injected into the vCA1 and LS of SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice at P45–P50, respectively. After 6 weeks, EPSCs evoked by two light (2 ms) pulses at 20 Hz were recorded in SST+-dLS or CB+-vLS neurons in the presence of 50 μM PTX.

Social memory acquisition protocol for slice physiology. sEPSCs were recorded 2 weeks after viral injection, while optogenetically evoked vCA1-LS EPSCs were recorded 6 weeks after viral injection. Briefly, subject mice were individually habituated in clean cages for 25 min per day for 3 consecutive days prior to the experiments. On the fourth day, following a 10-min of habituation, a novel juvenile mouse was introduced to the cage, and the subject mouse was allowed to freely interact with the stranger mouse for 10 min. A control mouse was placed in a similar but empty cage for 10 min. After 5 min, subject mice from the control and social groups were euthanized for slice physiology.

Rotarod running protocol for slice physiology. Two weeks after viral injection, all mice underwent training to run on a rotating rotarod (8r/min) for 10 min, followed by a 5-min stationary period. The training was conducted daily for three consecutive days. On the fourth day, after environmental adaptation, mice were assigned to either the running group (rotating rod, 8r/min) or the control group (stationary rod). Both groups remained on the rod for 10 min, followed by an additional 5-min stationary period. Mice that completed the full 15-min without dropping were euthanized for slice physiology.

Morphological reconstruction and analysis. For labeling the recorded neurons, we included biocytin (0.2%) in the K-gluconate-based internal solution. After recordings, slices with biocytin-labeled cells were post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight at 4 ℃. The slices were washed in 0.01 M PBS three times, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 for 1 h at RT, then incubated in Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated streptavidin (1:1 000, #S11223, Invitrogen) for 2 h at RT. For three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of labeled cells, z-stack images (0.5 μm/image) were acquired with a confocal microscope and processed using Fiji ImageJ as described previously103.

Statistical analysis

All statistics were calculated using GraphPad Prism v8 or Matlab R2021. All values in the text and figure legends are presented as mean ± SEM. Data analysis was performed by experimenters blind to experimental conditions. Normality of data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test, and equality of variances was checked using the Brown-Forsythe test. For unpaired non-parametric data, two-tailed Mann-Whitney test was used as indicated. For unpaired parametric data with unequal variance, two-tailed Welch's t-test was used to compare pairwise differences. For unpaired parametric data with equal variance, we applied two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test or one-way Repeated measures (RM) analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Holm–Sidak post-hoc test to examine pairwise differences. For normalized data compared to baseline mean, the two-tailed one-sample t-test was used for parametric data, and one-sample Wilcoxon signed rank test for non-parametric data.
