## Methods

Animals. All experimental procedures were performed following protocols approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of Huazhong University of Science and Technology, China. The SST-ires-Cre (SST-Cre), SST-ires-Flp (SST-Flp), CB-ires-Cre (CB-Cre), Rosa26-LSL-tdTomato (Ai14), Esr1-2a-Cre (Esr1-Cre) and Rosa26-LSL-H2B-GFP (LSL-H2B-GFP) mouse lines were imported from the Jackson Laboratory (SST-Cre: #013044; SST-Flp: #028579; CB-Cre: #028532; Ai14: #007914; Esr1-Cre: #0017913; LSL-H2B-GFP: #036761; JAX Mice and Services, USA). The C57BL/6 mice were purchased from the Animal Center of Huazhong University of Science and Technology. Mice (3–5 per cage) were housed under a 12-h light/dark cycle at an ambient temperature of 20–24 °C and relative humidity of 30–70%, with food and water provided ad libitum. We have only used male mice in this study because the social behaviors of laboratory mice exhibit sex- and strain-dependent behavioral parameters90,91.

Single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq)

Tissue collection and snRNA-seq. Single nuclei were isolated as described previously92. The LS was micro-dissected from six male C57BL/6 mice (2-month-old). Coronal LS sections (300-μm thick) spanning bregma +1.10 mm to −0.10 mm (Allen Brain Atlas, atlas.brain-map.org) were prepared with a vibratome, and four consecutive slices were collected. To minimize contamination from adjacent regions (e.g., MS, NAc, striatum, and corpus callosum), LS tissue was carefully isolated under a dissection microscope using a fine angled knife (#10056-12, FST) and fine forceps. Surrounding brain regions were removed, leaving only the LS (highlighted in purple in Supplementary Fig. 1a) for analysis. Tissues were rapidly frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until processing.

For single-nuclear suspension, tissues were thawed and homogenized in homogenization buffer containing 250 mM sucrose, 25 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl , 10 mM Tris, 0.1 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), mini protease 2 inhibitor cocktail (#11836153001; Roche, Switzerland), 0.4 U/μL RNase inhibitor, 1% BSA, and 0.1% NP40. Samples were centrifuged (500 g, 5 min, 4 ℃), washed with homogenization buffer, and repetitively pipetted to generate a nuclear suspension. The nuclear suspensions were again centrifuged (500 g, 5 min, 4 ℃) and resuspended in cold 1 × phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). After nucleus counting, the DNBSEQTM technology platform (BGI Genomics, China) and DNBelab C4 Single-Cell Library Prep Set (#1000021082; MGI, China) were used for snRNA-seq library preparation93. Briefly, the single-nucleus suspensions were converted to barcoded libraries using droplet generation, emulsion breakage, bead collection, reverse transcription, cDNA amplification, and purification. Indexed sequencing libraries were constructed according to the manufacturer’s protocols. Sequencing library quality was evaluated using a QubitTM ssDNA Assay Kit (#Q10212; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). Libraries were sequenced using an ultra-high-throughput DIPSEQ T1 sequencer with the following strategy: 30 bp for read 1, inclusive of 10 bp cell barcode 1, 10 bp cell barcode 2, and 10 bp unique molecular identifier (UMI), 100 bp of transcript sequence for read 2, and 10 bp for sample index.

SnRNA-seq data processing. Raw sequencing reads were filtered and demultiplexed using PISA (https://github.com/shiquan/PISA)94. Reads were aligned to the GRCm38 mouse genome using STAR (v2.7.4a) and sorted by Sambamba (v0.7.0).

Cell clustering and cell type identification. Cell clustering was performed using the Seurat (v4.1.0) R toolkit (https://github.com/satijalab/seurat). Qualified cells were filtered according to number of detected genes (between 500 and 6 500) and percentage of mitochondrial genes (< 0.1%). Genes expressed in < 3 cells were removed. The filtered dataset was log-normalized and scaled, and principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted. The first 18 PCs were used for graph-based clustering in Seurat using the Louvain algorithm. Non-neuronal clusters were identified by expression of Pdgfra, Oligo1, Mki67, Slc1a3, Mal, C1qa, Foxj1, and Cldn5 (Supplementary Fig. 1). A cluster with high mitochondrial gene expression and low detected genes was removed (data not shown). The remaining neuronal cells were then reclustered and processed using the same pipeline. Clusters were designated “non-LS” only if they expressed more than ten well-established markers for neighboring regions (e.g., MS, NAc) (Supplementary Fig. 2). Corresponding in-situ hybridization (ISH) images were adapted from Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, mouse.brain-map.org, and details are provided in Supplementary Table 3. Analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in all neuronal clusters was performed using the FindAllMarkers function in Seurat. Fold-changes and p-values of gene expression between Sst+ and Calb1+ clusters were calculated using the FindMarkers function with the MAST algorithm95.

Immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis. Mice were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane, then perfused with PBS followed by 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Brains were dissected and post-fixed in 4% PFA for 6 h at 4 °C, then immersed in 30% sucrose for 2 days before sectioning (30 μm) on a cryostat (Leica CM1050; Leica Biosystems, Germany). For IHC, slices were pre-incubated in blocking solution (10% normal goat serum with 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) for 1 h at room temperature (RT) and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies, including rabbit anti-CB (1:500, #14479-1-AP; Proteintech, China), mouse anti-NeuN (1:1 000, #MAB377; Merck, Germany), guinea pig anti-c-fos (1:1 000, #226004; SYSY, Germany), rabbit anti-RGS14 (1:1 000, #16258-1-AP; Proteintech, China), rat anti-mCherry (1:1 000, #M11217; Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA), and rabbit anti-GFP (1:1 000, #A-11122; Thermo Fisher Scientific). The slices were washed in PBS (10 min, three times) and incubated with secondary antibodies (1:1 000, goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 488, goat anti-rat Alexa Fluor 546, goat anti-guinea pig Alexa Fluor 633, and goat anti-mouse Alexa Fluor 647; Invitrogen, USA) for 2 h at RT. Next, the slices were mounted on positive-charged glass slides, coverslipped, and imaged using a confocal microscope (LSM 780, Carl Zeiss, Germany). The images were analyzed using Fiji ImageJ v1.52n.

c-fos labeling. Two-month-old male SST-Cre/Ai14 mice were singly housed in clean cages for 7 days before the experiment, then randomly divided into test and control groups. A test mouse was placed into a clean cage with a novel juvenile mouse. A control mouse was placed into an empty cage. After 10 min, mice from both groups were returned to their home cages for 1.5 h, then perfused with 4% PFA for IHC analysis (as above). All unbiased analyses were done manually from blinded groups.

Single-molecule fluorescent in-situ hybridization (smFISH). Two-month-old male mice were used for all experiments. Hybridization chain reaction (HCR) was used to detect mRNA expressions of Sst, Gad1 and Slc17a696. We designed probes targeting the coding and 3′UTR regions of Sst, Gad1 and Slc17a6 (Sangon Biotech, China). All solutions used for hybridization were prepared using RNase-free reagents and diethylpyrocarbonate (DEPC)-treated double deionized water (ddH O). After perfusion, brains were post-fixed in 4% PFA for 24 h, dehydrated in 20%–30% DEPC-treated sucrose for 24 h, cryosectioned (30 μm), and mounted onto SuperFrost glass slides. The sections were then immersed in 70% ethanol for 16 h at 4 °C, permeabilized by 0.5% Triton X-100 for 1 h at 37 °C, and treated with 10 µg/mL protease K to improve mRNA accessibility. After twice washing in 1 × PBS at RT, the brain sections were pre-hybridized in probe hybridization buffer for 10 min at 37 °C and further incubated with HCR probe (10 µM, Supplementary Table 1) at 37 °C for 3 h. After mRNA hybridization, washing and amplification procedures were conducted as described previously96.

RNAscope-FISH. Tissue preparation for RNAscope-FISH followed the same protocol as smFISH. Brains were cryosectioned into 20-μm sections and mounted onto SuperFrost glass slides. RNAscope-FISH was performed using the RNAscope v2 Assay kit (cat. #323100, Advanced Cell Diagnostics, USA), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The following target probes were used: Sst (cat. #404631-C1), Calb1 (cat. #428431-C2), Nts (cat. #420441-C3), Prlr (cat. #430791-C3), Htr2c (cat. #401001-C3), and Glp1r (cat. #418851-C2). All probes were obtained from Advanced Cell Diagnostics (ACDBio, USA).

Virus preparation. Two AAV serotypes (AAV2/9 and AAV2-retro) were used. AAV2-retro was used to retrogradely label projection neurons in the vCA197. The plasmid for AAV-DIO-EGFP-2A-TeNT was a gift from Dr. Thomas C. Südhof (Stanford University). All AAVs (AAV-DIO-EGFP, AAV-DIO-tdTomato, AAV-DIO-mCherry, AAV-fDIO-H2B-mCherry, AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry, AAV-DIO-EGFP-2A-TeNT, AAV-DIO-hM3Dq-mCherry, AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato, AAV-DIO-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV-fDIO-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV-CaMKII-ChR2(H134R)-EYFP, AAV-Syn-Cre-off-eNpHR3.0-mCherry, AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-EGFP, AAV2-retro-Syn-Cre-tdTomato, AAV-CaMKll-eArchT3.0-EGFP, AAV-Syn-DIO-TVA-2a-RG-2a-mCherry), and the SAD ΔG-GFP pseudotyped rabies virus were purchased from Shanghai Taitool Bioscience (China) or Brain Case (China). The final viral vector titers of AAVs ranged from 3 to 8 × 1012 particles/mL. The final titer of the SAD ΔG-GFP pseudotyped rabies virus was 108 infecting units/mL.

Stereotaxic injection. Mice were anesthetized with tribromoethanol (150–250 mg/kg, i.p.). Standard surgery was performed to expose the brain surface above the LS or ventral hippocampus. Coordinates for the LS injections in SST-Cre were: bregma 0.86 mm, lateral ±0.35 mm, and dura −2.5 mm. Coordinates for the LS injections in CB-Cre were: bregma 0.5 mm, lateral ±0.37 mm, and dura −3.0 mm. Coordinates for hippocampal vCA1d injection were: bregma −3.28 mm, lateral ±3.10 mm, dura −1.4 mm. Coordinates for hippocampal vCA1v injection were: bregma −3.28 mm, lateral ±3.10 mm, dura −3.4 mm. AAVs (200–400 nL) were stereotaxically injected using a glass pipette connected to a Nanoliter Injector MICRO-2T (World Precision Instruments, Inc., USA) at a slow flow rate of 0.12 μL/min. The pipette was withdrawn at least 10 min after the viral injection. AAV-DIO-EGFP, AAV-DIOS-tdTomato, or AAV-DIO-mCherry were bilaterally injected into the LS of SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice for control experiments. Experimental designs related to viral injection are summarized in Supplementary Table 2. Schematics of injection sites in the main and supplementary figures were adapted from reference brain images from Allen Mouse Brain Atlas, atlas.brain-map.org.

Optical fiber implantation. Three weeks after AAV injection, ceramic ferrules with an optical fiber (200-μm diameter, N.A. 0.37, Inper Inc., China) were bilaterally implanted with the fiber tips on the top of the dLS (bregma 0.86 mm, lateral ±1.10 mm, and dura −2.55 mm) at a 14° angle and the vLS (bregma 0.5 mm, lateral ±1.47 mm, and dura −3.0 mm) at a 14° angle, the vCA1 (bregma−3.28 mm, lateral ± 3.5 mm, and dura −2.65 mm), the NAc (bregma 1.42 mm, lateral ± 1.07 mm, and dura −3.46 mm) at a 8° angle, the POA (bregma −0.10 mm, lateral ± 1.3 mm, and dura −4.6 mm) at a 10° angle, the AHN (bregma −0.82 mm, lateral ± 1.25 mm, and dura −4.5 mm) at a 8° angle, and the LHA (bregma −2.06 mm, lateral ± 1.0 mm, and dura −5.0 mm). The ferrules were secured onto the skull with dental cement. Optogenetic experiments were performed at least 6 weeks after AAV injection. The tip of the optical fiber was usually located 100~500 μm above the AAV injection center. Only mice with a correct injection sites and optical fiber tracks above the target regions were included in the analyses. Animals with off-target injections or misplaced fibers were excluded, and the number of exclusions is reported in Supplementary Table 4. In very rare cases, control mice with abnormal brain structures (e.g., cerebral edema) were also excluded.

Optogenetic manipulation. The optical fiber cable was connected via patch cords and 1 × 2 Fiber-optic Rotary Joints (Doric Lenses, Canada) to a laser (Shanghai Dream Lasers Technology, China). For ChR2 activation, blue laser pulses (473 nm, 5, 10, or 20 Hz, 5 ms/pulse) were applied during certain behavioral stages. For ArchT silencing, a continuous green laser (532 nm) was applied. Laser power at the optical fiber tip was measured with a power meter (PM100D, Thorlabs, USA) and calibrated to 10 mW/mm2.

Chemogenetic manipulation. For chemogenetic manipulation of LS CB+ neurons, CB-Cre mice were injected with AAV-DIO-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry or AAV-DIO-mCherry (Control). Clozapine-N-oxide (CNO, 5 mg/kg dissolved in saline; #4936, Tocris Bioscience, UK) or saline was i.p. injected 30 min prior to behavioral tests.

Mouse behaviors

Preparation for behavioral tests. Behavioral tests were performed at least 3 weeks after AAV injection. All animals were handled daily for 3 days in advance and habituated for 3 h in the test room before behavioral tests. All apparatuses were cleaned with 75% ethanol to eliminate odors. All behavioral tests were conducted in the light phase (10:00–19:00). All experiments were video-recorded and analyzed using a tracking system (Biobserve, Germany).

Open field test (OFT). White-colored plastic boxes (40 × 40 × 40 cm) were used as the open field chambers. Mice were individually placed into the center of the box and allowed to freely explore for 10 min. Total distance travelled, time spent in center arena (20 × 20 cm), distance travelled in center, and number of visits to center were analyzed.

Elevated plus maze (EPM). The maze consisted of two open arms (35 × 6 cm), two closed arms (35 × 6 × 15 cm), and a central connecting region (6 × 6 cm), positioned 45 cm above the ground. Mice were individually placed in the central region with their head facing the open arm and allowed to freely explore for 5 min. Time spent and number of entries in the open arms vs. closed arms were recorded.

Novel object recognition test-1 (NORT-1). NORT was conducted to evaluate non-social recognition ability, as previously described98. For the training phase, two identical objects (blue cylindrical glass bottles) were symmetrically placed in the open field chamber. Each mouse was allowed to freely explore the objects for 10 min, then returned to its home cage. After 1 h, a novel object (gray cubic brick) was used to randomly replace one of the familiar objects. The test mouse was returned to the chamber and time spent interacting with the objects was recorded. We cumulatively counted the first 20 s that the mouse interacted with the two objects. The discrimination index was calculated by: (T – T ) / (T + T ), where T and T represent time spent exploring novel and familiar objects, respectively.

Novel object recognition test-2 (NORT-2). This test was adapted as previously described15. For the habituation phase, the subject mouse was introduced into the open field chamber for 5 min. Then two identical objects (blue cylindrical glass bottles) were symmetrically placed in opposite corners of the open field chamber. Each mouse was allowed to freely explore the objects for 10 min (learning phase), then returned to its home cage. After 30 min, a novel object (gray cubic brick) was used to randomly replace one of the familiar objects. The test mouse was returned to the chamber and were allowed to explore for 5 minutes. The discrimination index was calculated by: (T – T ) / (T + T ), where T and T represent time spent exploring novel and familiar objects, respectively, during the 5-min period.

Three-chamber social test. The classical three-chamber social test was performed as previously described2. The apparatus was divided into three chambers (30 × 30 × 30 cm), with connecting doors. Two cylinders (5-cm circular base radius and 15-cm height) were placed in the middle of the side chambers. The behavioral test consisted of three sessions, including habituation (10 min), sociability test (10 min), and social memory test (10 min). During habituation, the test mouse was allowed to freely explore the arena for 10 min. For the familiarization session, a novel stranger mouse (age and sex matched, stranger 1) was randomly placed in the left or right cylinder, with the other cylinder empty. The subject mouse was allowed to explore the two cylinders (with or without stranger 1) for 10 min. Interaction time was defined as the time in which the subject mouse spent investigating each cylinder (snout within 2 cm of the mesh barrier), as described previously2. The social index was calculated by: social index = (T – T ) / (T + T ), where T and T represent interaction time for the two cylinders, respectively. For the social memory test session, a novel stranger mouse (stranger 2) was randomly placed in the left or right cylinder, and the now familiar mouse (stranger 1) was placed in the other cylinder. The test mouse was allowed to explore the two cylinders (with novel or familiar stranger) for 10 min. Interaction time towards the familiar mouse (S1) and novel mouse (S2) was recorded. The social discrimination (SD) index was calculated by: SDI = (T – T ) / (T + T ). For most experiments, there was no interval between the familiarization and social memory test sessions. For the prolonged social memory test, the social memory session was performed after an interval of 10–60 min (Supplementary Fig. 11g) or 40 min (Fig. 2l and 4f).

For the social memory experiments related to vCA1 (Fig. 6; Supplementary Fig. 21), a novel stranger mouse (age- and sex-matched, stranger 1) and a novel object (blue brick, 4 × 4 × 6 cm) were randomly placed in the left or right cylinder during the familiarization session. The social memory test session was carried out after an interval of 10 min.

For the two-round social memory test (Supplementary Fig 12), we introduced a 10‑min interval between the first social memory recall (S1 vs. S2) and the subsequent social memory acquisition (S3).

5-trial social memory assay. This test was performed as previously described 2,15. The test mouse was placed in a clean cage for a 4-h habituation period. Subsequently, a novel mouse (5-6 weeks old) was introduced into the cage for four consecutive 1-min trials with a 10-min inter-trial interval. On the fifth trial, a second novel stimulus animal was presented. The direct interaction time was analyzed frame by frame from the video using a Matlab code as previously described53.

Real-time conditioned place preference (RT-CPP). The RT-CPP apparatus consisted of two adjacent chambers (20 × 30 × 30 cm), which were visually (black and white) and tactilely (smooth and rough) different. One chamber was randomly assigned as the initial photostimulated side (phase 1). After 10 min, the stimulated side was switched to the previously non-stimulated chamber (phase 2). In each session, a mouse with optical fibers was placed into the non-photostimulated side and allowed to freely explore the two side chambers. Each time the mouse entered the photostimulated side, green (532 nm) light was delivered until the mouse returned to the non-photostimulated side. There was no interruption between phase 1 and phase 2. Time spent in each chamber (stimulated vs. non-stimulated) was recorded, and preference for the photostimulated side was calculated by: preference = percentage of time spent in photostimulated side – percentage of time spent in non-photostimulated side.

Pseudotyped rabies virus-mediated retrograde tracing and AAV-mediated anterograde tracing. For retrograde tracing, we first unilaterally injected 80 nL of AAV-Syn-DIO-TVA-2a-RG-2a-mCherry into the dLS of SST-Cre or the vLS of CB-Cre mice, respectively. Three weeks later, 300 nL of RV-ΔG-GFP (glycoprotein deficient, GFP-expressing rabies virus) was injected into the same location under biosafety level 2 conditions as above. One week after RV -ΔG-GFP injection, mice were euthanized and their brains were collected. For anterograde tracing, AAV-DIO-EGFP (50 nL) were unilaterally injected into the dLS of SST-Cre or the vLS of CB-Cre mice, respectively. Coronal slices (40 μm) were cryosectioned as above, and every third section was collected for imaging analysis. Fluorescence images were acquired with a SV120 Olympus automatic slide scanner (10× objective, 0.4 NA, Japan).

To quantify rabies virus (RV) labeled neurons along the dorsal-to-ventral axis of vCA1, we adapted a previously described method99. Briefly, A spline curve was first drawn along the vCA1 pyramidal layer from its dorsal to ventral end and divided into 100 equal segments. RV-labeled neurons were then counted within each segment. Vertical boundaries for each segment were defined by the tangent to the spline at the corresponding point. In Fig. 5d, the X-axis (0–100) represents the relative position along the vCA1 dorsal–ventral axis, where 0 denotes the most dorsal region and 100 the most ventral region.

In-vivo electrophysiology

In-vivo single-unit recordings and data analysis. In-vivo electrophysiological recordings were performed in freely moving or head-fixed mice as per previous study53,59. Opto-electrodes (optrodes) consisted of a custom-designed miniature micro-drive containing 16 movable electrodes (25.4-μm nickel-chromium wire, #761500; A-M System, USA) and an optical fiber in the center. Final resistance of the electrodes was 700–800 kΩ. AAV-DIO-ArchT-tdTomato was bilaterally injected into the LS of 7–8-week-old SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice. Three weeks later, mice were anesthetized with tribromoethanol (150–250 mg/kg, i.p.) and placed in a stereotaxic frame. The mice were properly aligned and the optrodes were implanted into the LS. Dental cement was applied to fully cover the exposed skull and secure the implants. After surgery, mice were returned to their home cage and allowed to recover for at least 10 days before recording.

To record single-unit activity in freely moving mice (Supplementary Fig. 9b), we recorded neuronal activity during social interactions100. First, the experimental mouse was placed in the test arena (40 × 40 × 40 cm) for 5 min to record baseline activity. A novel stranger mouse was then introduced to the chamber. Both mice were separated by a plastic wall with small holes (7.5 mm) (Fig. 3b; Supplementary Fig. 9b), which allowed social interaction with each other. Neuronal activity was recorded for another 5 or 20 min during social interaction. Wide-band (WB) signals were recorded for offline sorting and mouse behaviors were videotaped simultaneously for further analysis.

To record single-unit activity in head-fixed mice (Supplementary Fig. 9j-m), we used a previously established recording setup53, in which mice were head-fixed using a 3D-printed head ring and allowed to run freely on a wheel. Each mouse was presented with either an anesthetized stranger mouse (male, 5-6 weeks old) or a novel object (3 × 3 × 3 cm) placed on a movable platform. Once positioned, the stimulus was approximately 0.5 cm from the nose of the recording mouse. For SST+ neuron recordings during social interactions, the stimulus was presented for 5 s with 25 s intervals, repeated for 20 trials.

To record mutual inhibition during social interactions in vivo (Supplementary Fig. 16), neuronal activity was recorded during a 10-min baseline period or a 10-min social interaction period, during which an anesthetized male mouse was continuously presented. Optogenetic stimulation (λ = 532 nm, 3 s pulses, 10 s inter-pulse interval, 20 trials) was delivered within 1 minute of each recording condition.

Single-unit sorting was performed manually by Offline Sorter v4.0 (Plexon, Inc., USA). Spiking activities were digitized at 40 kHz and stored for offline sorting. The WB signals were high-pass filtered at 250 Hz and waveform detection thresholds were placed at -4.0 to -4.5 times the standard error of digital signal range, depending on the signal-noise ratio. The detected waveforms were aligned at the valley point, and two-dimensional principal component analysis (PCA) was used for separation of single-unit spikes. The distribution of inter-spike intervals (ISIs) from all isolated single-unit spikes exhibited recognizable refractory periods (> 1 ms). Only well-isolated units (L ratio < 0.2, isolation distance > 15) were included for analyses.

In-vivo firing rate analysis. Single-unit responses were analyzed using NeuroExplorer v5.0 (Plexon, Inc.). Well-separated single-unit spikes were collected to analyze neuronal responses to social stimuli. During 20-min social interactions, the start and end time points of each social bout were manually labeled by examining behavioral videos frame by frame. The ISIs of single-unit spikes during baseline and social interaction were compared to evaluate significant firing rate differences (p < 0.05, two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test). The mean and SD during the total recorded time were used for calculating firing rate Z-score. Neurons were considered as activated with a firing rate Z-score value > 2.0 during the 3 s of stimulus presentation101.

In-vivo cell type identification. To identify SST+ and CB+ single units, we utilized ArchT-mediated optic tagging102, whereby laser pulses (λ = 532 nm, 3 s long) were delivered via the optical fiber after each behavioral recording session (Supplementary Fig. 9).

In-vivo local field potential recording. Optrodes containing two-channel single electrodes (75-μm stainless steel wire, #793400; A-M System, USA) and an optical fiber were hand-made as described previously59. Local field potentials (LFPs) were sampled at 1 kHz with a low-pass filter at 250 Hz. The LFP power spectra across four frequency bands, including alpha (1–3 Hz), theta (4–12 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), and gamma (31–80 Hz), were analyzed. Power spectrum density (PSD) was calculated using NeuroExplorer v5.0 (Plexon Inc.). For optogenetic manipulation during LFP recordings, 5-ms blue light pulses (5, 10, and 20 Hz, λ = 473 nm) were used to activate SST+ neurons, whereas continuous green light (λ = 532 nm) was delivered to inhibit SST+ neurons or the vCA1d→dLS pathway.

In-vivo phase locking analysis. Single units and LFP recorded by the 16-channel optrode were used for phase-lock analysis to evaluate the relationship between theta oscillations and timestamps in SST+ and CB+ neurons in the LS, as described previously58,59. The oscillatory activity phase was extracted using Hilvert’s transformation and converted into angle degrees. Rayleigh test was used for circular uniformity to identify significant correlations between the timing of spikes and specific phase of the theta cycle58,59.

Slice electrophysiology and optogenetics. Mice were euthanized with isoflurane and coronal LS, AHN, or LHA slices (300-μm thick) were sectioned with a vibratome (VT1200S; Leica Biosystems, Germany) in cutting solution containing (in mM): 228 sucrose, 2.5 KCI, 26 NaHCO , 1 NaH PO ·2H O, 11 D-Glucose, 0.5 CaCl , and 7 MgCl , then transferred to artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) containing (in mM): 119 NaCl, 2.5 KCI, 26 NaHCO , 1 NaH PO ·2H O, 11 D-Glucose, 2.5 CaCl , and 1.3 MgCl (pH = 7.4). Slices were incubated at 35 °C for 30 min and then at RT until use. Recordings were performed in a submerged-style chamber mounted under an infrared-differential interference contrast (IR-DIC) microscope (BX-51 WI; Olympus, Japan). Whole-cell recordings were performed using a MultiClamp 700B amplifier and Digidata 1550B4 (Molecular Devices, USA). Patch pipette resistance was 4–6 MΩ. Signals were sampled at 20 kHz, filtered at 10 kHz, and analyzed using Clampex v10.4 (Molecular Devices).

To analyze electrophysiological properties, SST+ and CB+ neurons were visualized by tdTomato expression in SST-Cre/Ai14 or CB-Cre/Ai14 mice, respectively. TdTomato+ neurons were recorded with a K-gluconate-based internal solution containing (in mM): 135 K-gluconate, 10 HEPES, 8 KCl, 0.25 EGTA, 0.3 Na GTP, 2 MgATP, 7 phospho-creatine, and 0.1 spermine (pH 7.25–7.3; osmolarity 294–298). To compare the neuronal excitability, the recorded neurons were subjected to step current injections with different amplitudes ranging from 20 to 160 pA, and the number of action potentials (APs) was counted accordingly. To record HCN-mediated sag amplitudes, the recorded neurons were subjected to step current injections with different amplitudes ranging from –80 pA to –20 pA, and the sag amplitudes were estimated by subtracting the values at the onset of hyperpolarizing voltages (peak amplitude) from those at the end (steady-state) as previously described52.

For recording IPSCs from SST+ neurons, AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP was bilaterally injected into the LS of SST-Cre/Ai14 mice at postnatal day 35–40 (P35–P40). After 6 weeks, tdTomato-/EYFP- neurons (presumably Cre- neurons) in the LS were recorded using a KCl-based internal solution containing (in mM): 71 KCl, 72 K-gluconate, 10 HEPES, 2 MgCl , 0.025 BAPTA, and 2 MgATP (pH 7.25–7.3; osmolarity 295–300). To study inhibitory synapses from CB+ to SST+ neurons, AAV-DIO-ChR2-EYFP and AAV-fDIO-H2B-mCherry were bilaterally injected into the LS of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice at P35–P40. After 6 weeks, mCherry+ neurons (SST+ neurons) in the LS were recorded with the same KCl-based internal solution. Light (2 ms)-evoked IPSCs were recorded in the presence of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP, 50 μM; #0940, Tocris) and tetrodotoxin (TTX, 1 μM; #1078, Tocris). D-(-)-2-amino-5-phosphonopentanoic acid (D-AP5, 50 μM; #0106, Tocris) and 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione disodium (CNQX, 20 μM; #1045, Tocris) or picrotoxin (PTX, 50 μM; #1128, Tocris) were perfused with ACSF to examine the neurotransmitter type used by ChR2-EYFP-expressing neurons. The inhibitory synapses from SST+ to CB+ neurons were also studied by injecting AAV-fDIO-ChR2-EYFP and AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry into the LS of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice. The SST+-dLS→LHA and CB+-vLS→AHN pathways were also validated as mentioned above.

For dual patch-clamp recordings, AAV-CaMKII-ChR2-EYFP was bilaterally injected into the vCA1d or vCA1v of CB-Cre/SST-Flp mice at P35–P40. After 6 weeks, SST+ neurons in the dLS and CB+ neurons in the vLS were recorded using the K-gluconate-based internal solution. Light-induced excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) were recorded in SST+ and CB+ neurons simultaneously.

For sEPSC recordings, AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry was bilaterally injected into the LS of SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice at P45–P50. After two weeks, SST+ neurons in the dLS and CB+ neurons in the vLS were recorded using a CsMeSO -based internal solution (in mM): 140 CsMeSO , 10 HEPES, 8 CsCl, 0.25 EGTA, 0.3 Na GTP, 2 MgATP, 7 phospho-creatine, and 0.1 spermine (pH 7.25–7.3; osmolarity 295–300). The sEPSCs were recorded with 50 μM PTX in ACSF.

For recording the PPRs of vCA1-LS EPSCs, AAV-CaMKII-ChR2-EYFP and AAV-DIO-H2B-mCherry were bilaterally injected into the vCA1 and LS of SST-Cre or CB-Cre mice at P45–P50, respectively. After 6 weeks, EPSCs evoked by two light (2 ms) pulses at 20 Hz were recorded in SST+-dLS or CB+-vLS neurons in the presence of 50 μM PTX.

Social memory acquisition protocol for slice physiology. sEPSCs were recorded 2 weeks after viral injection, while optogenetically evoked vCA1-LS EPSCs were recorded 6 weeks after viral injection. Briefly, subject mice were individually habituated in clean cages for 25 min per day for 3 consecutive days prior to the experiments. On the fourth day, following a 10-min of habituation, a novel juvenile mouse was introduced to the cage, and the subject mouse was allowed to freely interact with the stranger mouse for 10 min. A control mouse was placed in a similar but empty cage for 10 min. After 5 min, subject mice from the control and social groups were euthanized for slice physiology.

Rotarod running protocol for slice physiology. Two weeks after viral injection, all mice underwent training to run on a rotating rotarod (8r/min) for 10 min, followed by a 5-min stationary period. The training was conducted daily for three consecutive days. On the fourth day, after environmental adaptation, mice were assigned to either the running group (rotating rod, 8r/min) or the control group (stationary rod). Both groups remained on the rod for 10 min, followed by an additional 5-min stationary period. Mice that completed the full 15-min without dropping were euthanized for slice physiology.

Morphological reconstruction and analysis. For labeling the recorded neurons, we included biocytin (0.2%) in the K-gluconate-based internal solution. After recordings, slices with biocytin-labeled cells were post-fixed in 4% PFA overnight at 4 ℃. The slices were washed in 0.01 M PBS three times, permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100 for 1 h at RT, then incubated in Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated streptavidin (1:1 000, #S11223, Invitrogen) for 2 h at RT. For three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of labeled cells, z-stack images (0.5 μm/image) were acquired with a confocal microscope and processed using Fiji ImageJ as described previously103.

Statistical analysis

All statistics were calculated using GraphPad Prism v8 or Matlab R2021. All values in the text and figure legends are presented as mean ± SEM. Data analysis was performed by experimenters blind to experimental conditions. Normality of data was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test, and equality of variances was checked using the Brown-Forsythe test. For unpaired non-parametric data, two-tailed Mann-Whitney test was used as indicated. For unpaired parametric data with unequal variance, two-tailed Welch's t-test was used to compare pairwise differences. For unpaired parametric data with equal variance, we applied two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test or one-way Repeated measures (RM) analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Holm–Sidak post-hoc test to examine pairwise differences. For normalized data compared to baseline mean, the two-tailed one-sample t-test was used for parametric data, and one-sample Wilcoxon signed rank test for non-parametric data. In same-mouse or same-cell experiments, two-tailed paired Student’s t-test and two-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test were used for parametric and non-parametric two-paired data, respectively. Two-way RM ANOVA with Holm–Sidak post-hoc test was used to compare multiple related samples. Two-tailed Chi-squared test was used for comparing multiple composition ratios. Rayleigh test was used to identify significant correlations between the timing of spikes and specific phase of the theta cycle. Two-tailed Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was used to analyze the statistical significance of the cumulative distribution of sEPSC amplitudes or inter-event intervals in slice electrophysiology. Detailed statistical analyses are provided in Supplementary Table 5. Significance notation: n.s., not significant; *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001; #p < 0.05, ##p < 0.01, ###p < 0.001.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This study investigated the two parallel downstream circuits of ventral CA1, which has been shown to be the center of social memory, that are critical for social memory acquisition but not for social memory retrieval. The involvement of two circuits, vCA1d-SST+-dLS-lateral hypothalamic area and vCA1v-CB+-vLS-anterior hypothalamic nucleus, has been beautifully demonstrated using chemogenetic/optogenetic manipulation and electrophysiology. The results are very clear and strongly support the conclusions, so it is a study of exceptionally high scientific value to understand neural mechanisms underlying social memory. I have several concerns and suggestions to improve the paper.
1. While there is no doubt that the brain region referred to as vCA1v is indeed vCA1, the region referred to as vCA1d is unclear from the coronal section whether it is CA1 or CA2. This is particularly important because dLS receives especially strong neural projections from the CA2 region, making it necessary to clarify this point. Therefore, in addition to the coronal sections, horizontal sections should be shown, and co-staining with CA2 marker genes such as RGS14 should be conducted.
2. Some of the data in this paper are related to the following study recently published in eLife. It is necessary to clearly highlight the differences between the two in the discussion section and to cite the study appropriately.
“A ventral hippocampal-lateral septum pathway regulates social novelty preference. Rashid et al., https://elifesciences.org/reviewed-preprints/97259”
3. Regarding Figure 4 and Supplementary Figure 11, the SST+ neurons and CB+ neurons are shown to inhibit each other bilaterally. It is also suggested that they contribute to social memory performance as shown in Figure 8, partially supported by the SST+ (but not CB+) neurons contributing to enhanced theta oscillations (Figure 3) and presynaptic potentiation in vCA1d-SST+-dLS (but not in vCA1v-CB+-vLS) (Figure 6). This seems to indicate that positive regulation by SST+ neurons is stronger than negative regulation by CB+ neurons. Could the authors discuss these asymmetric results more, possibly from the viewpoint of the balance between bilateral inhibition? Furthermore, given the presynaptic potentiation in vCA1d-SST+-dLS, the results that vCA1-LS pathways are not important for social memory retrieval are counterintuitive. What could be the potential mechanism to explain this?
4. The authors showed that the vCA1-LS circuit is important for social memory acquisition but not recall, and the vCA1-NAc circuit is important for social memory recall but not acquisition (Supplementary Figure 15). According to Gergues et al. (Nature Neuroscience 23:1444, 2020), it has been shown that there are many neurons projecting to both LS and NAc. Are these dual-projecting neurons involved in social memory regulation shown in this study? Or are the single-projecting neurons involved?

### Reviewer 2

I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

### Reviewer 3

In this study, Zhang et al. investigated the role of two distinctive LS subpopulations- SST- and CB-expressing LS neurons- in bidirectional control of social memory acquisition. Using single nucleus RNA sequencing and immunostaining, they observed that SST- and CB-expressing LS neurons have molecularly and anatomically distinctive characteristics. The authors then demonstrated that each population positively and negatively regulates social memory acquisition, respectively. Optogenetic experiments further highlighted that this regulation is specifically engaged in social memory acquisition, but not social memory recall or sociability per se. Notably, SST LS neurons play a critical role in regulating socially relevant theta oscillations. At the circuit level, the dorsal and ventral LS (dLS, vLS) receive inputs from distinct parts of the hippocampus along its dorsal-ventral axis. Circuit-specific optogenetic manipulation revealed that vCA1d>dLS and vCA1v>vLS pathway can control social memory acquisition in a bidirectional way, similar to the effects observed after manipulating SST- and CB-expressing neurons, predominantly located in dorsal and ventral part of LS, respectively. The authors went one step further to demonstrate that the LHA and AHN are critical downstream targets of SST-and CB-expressing LS neurons to regulate social memory acquisition. Overall, this study provides valuable information into how specific neuronal circuits connecting the hippocampus to LS influence the social memory process. However, inconsistencies in data hinder in-dept interpretation, and generating superficial conclusions, primarily based on the results from artificial manipulation, is insufficient to support publication at this time. To further improve the paper, more clarifications listed below would be helpful.
Here are some specific comments:
1. In Figure 1, snRNA seq results show that SST- and CB-expressing LS neurons display distinct molecular profiles with different expression levels for Nts, Glp1r, Htr2c and Prlr. Has this result been confirmed using other methods, such as in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry?
2. The author claimed that previous studies demonstrated the ‘controversial’ role of the LS in social behaviors (line #55, 139), but it is unclear what it meant by ‘controversial’ in this context. Given the heterogeneity of LS cell types, several studies have been descriptive, focusing on different populations of LS and highlighting their functional relevance on different domains of social behaviors. These studies do not necessarily appear to be inconsistent or in disagreement (controversial) with each other. Please clarify this point.
3. Figure 3 shows that theta oscillation power is increased during both social bouts and non-social intervals. Is this LS theta oscillation still sustained even after the social stimuli are removed, or is it specifically engaged during the social context? The same question would be related to SST LS neurons: Is the proportion of theta phase-locked SST LS neurons unique to social contexts?
4. What is the explanation for using continuous social interaction tests for 20 min in Figure 3, instead of separate sessions of sociability vs. social novelty, as used throughout the rest of the paper? Figure 3e shows consistent enhancement of theta rhythm oscillations between P1 and P4 with no statistical difference as the familiarity is developed. More evidence is needed to substantiate their claim, this is a key neural mechanism for social memory acquisitions (line #220).
5. What is the justification for the lack of changes in the power of theta rhythm oscillations in response to 20 Hz-ChR2 activation of SST LS neurons in Figure 3m?
6. In Figure 5, TeNT silencing is applied to the vCA1d>dLS pathway using intersectional viral strategies. Given the collateral projections of vCA1 neurons, it is important to clarify whether the vCA1d>dLS pathway is a key participant for blocking the enhanced theta oscillations during social interaction in Supplementary Fig.14.
7. In Figure 5d, it is unclear what numbers (0~100) on the X axis represent regarding the dorsal-ventral axis of vCA1.
8. Supplementary Figure 6 shows that both SST- and CB-expressing LS neurons are activated by social stimuli, but this result is correlated with increased in vivo firing rate of SST LS neurons, but not with the one of CB LS neurons (Supplementary Fig. 7). Please discuss why.
9. Based on supplementary Fig. 9e, the authors claimed that inhibition of SST LS neurons did not produce rewarding or aversive effects, though there is a lack of interpretation for many data indicating reduced anxiety level after inhibiting SST LS neurons or SST dLS> LH circuitry in supplementary Fig. 8, 17. It is unclear to understand the situation that poor social memory and low anxiety are related to each other, given that high anxiety typically causes memory loss in real world situations.
10. The authors consistently claimed that SST LS and CB LS neuronal circuit exert ‘opposing’ effects on social memory, mainly based on results from artificial manipulation in Figures 2, 4 and 5. However, I’m unsure about the interpretation of ‘opposing role’, given that both SST- and CB-expressing LS neuronal populations are similarly activated by social stimuli (Supplementary Fig. 2). In addition, CB LS neuronal activity is not correlated with socially relevant theta oscillation (Supplementary Fig. 7), as well as frequency/amplitude of sEPSCs in CB LS neurons are not affected by social interaction (Figure 6), while SST LS neurons are largely engaged in both cases. Beyond the data from artificial manipulations, more physiological/endogenous evidence is needed to support the claim that SST LS and CB LS neuronal circuits oppose each other for regulating social memory acquisition.
11. In Discussion, the authors claimed that the opposing effects of vCA1d>SST dLS>LHA and vCA1>CB vLS> AHA on social memory may be explained by the predominantly GABAergic nature of AHN neurons and the predominantly glutamatergic nature of LHA neurons (line #532~534). What is the justification for this claim? Given previous studies suggesting that both AHN and LHA contain a decent amount of intermingled GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons, the authors need to provide more evidence in depth to support their explanation.
12. There are some misplaced figure annotations throughout which should be corrected.

### Reviewer 4

The authors present an interesting and important data set exploring the contributions of somatostatin (Sst) and calbindin 1 (Calb1)-expressing cells in the lateral septum (LS) to social behavior. The authors used single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) and histological preparations to show that Sst and Calb1 are largely nonoverlapping in the LS. The authors then use a variety of circuit manipulations to show that inhibition of Sst cells reduces social discrimination when performed at least during training; discrimination is increased with their stimulation. Inhibition of Sst cells appears to reduce theta power, while their activation increases it. Conversely, Calb1 manipulations show opposite effects. This may be due to inhibition of Sst cells by Calb1 neurons, as seen in their slice preparations. Additionally, Sst and Calb1 cells appear to have differential input from the hippocampus, based on rabies tracing and ex vivo electrophysiology. Inhibition of inputs from CA1d to the dLS during training reduced social discrimination, whereas social discrimination was disrupted by activation of CA1v inputs to the vLS, mirroring what was seen with Sst/Calb1 manipulations. Generally, the paper is well-written, the topic is interesting, and the cells and circuits involved are likely to be of high interest to many readers. The authors should be commended for their extensive dataset. However, my enthusiasm is deeply hindered by a surface-level discussion and analysis of the sequencing (there is little comparison of their findings with others who have previously sequenced the LS; some prior works are not cited) and of their other circuit mapping and behavioral experiments (others have also explored functions of Sst cells in the LS and little is discussed of this prior work). I expand on these concerns below:
MAJOR ITEMS (in no particular order):
---Theta power in the LS appears to similarly increase during both social and non-social events (Figure 3). While it appears Sst neurons phase lock to theta, it’s unclear then how Sst activity encodes social events. Did the authors observe single-unit activity of Sst cells during social bouts? Do they correlate with behavior? The authors also suggest that sociability itself was unaffected by the circuit manipulations, but is exploration of S1 higher in Sst-ArchT vs. controls (Supp. Figure 9)?
---Related to the above, socially interacting mice may locomote more than a mouse in a familiar empty cage. Is there any concern that the data in Supplementary Figure 6 and Figure 6 reflect differences in locomotion, which may be independent of “social” experience per se? In other words, would a similar outcome occur if mice were wheel-running or given other novel stimuli?
---Others have explored the function of Sst cells in the LS including in the OFT and EPM. For example, Besnard et al. 2019 did not find changes in OFT/EPM with optogenetic inhibition of Sst cells in the LS, however the authors here observed more time in the open arms with TeNT inactivation. Conversely, Besnard et al. 2019 observed more in time in the open arms of EPM with optogenetic stimulation, which may be in conflict with what the authors show here. These differences are not discussed/addressed.
---It is unclear to me whether appropriate stats are used. For most of the memory recall tests, it appears the authors used one t-test for controls and a separate one for experimental groups (comparing S1 to S2), without reporting any sort of ANOVA/interaction that directly compares controls with experimental mice. The authors use t-tests for the discrimination ratio, but this ratio should mirror the interaction found in the investigation times. I suspect ANOVAs may yield significant interactions that would merit these comparisons (that should be followed by appropriate posthocs), but currently many of the statistics appear to lack rigor. Similarly, I am unsure why Figure 3e (and similar panels) makes use of multiple t-tests in the absence of an ANOVA.
---This is not the first dataset to use snRNAseq to explore the diversity of LS cells. Surprisingly, the authors do not cite some of these prior works. This should be rectified. Moreover, very little effort is made to discuss how their data compare to these prior studies. Do the authors observe the same populations of cells in their dataset as others and in similar proportions? Why or why not?
---I find the designation of “non-LS” to certain clusters in the sequencing data to be a bold claim. The authors largely rely on in situ images from the Allen Brain to help establish whether cells may be “LS” or “non-LS”. This approach is limited as the in situ data may not capture the dynamic expression of these genes or may not have the resolution to account for sparse labeling in the septum (or low levels), or may be expressed in other parts of the septum that are simply not shown in the in situ images. It is entirely possible for putative LS cells to be found within clusters that the authors designate as “non-LS”, and this caveat or possibility is not addressed or discussed in the manuscript. For example, Coro6 is shown, and this appears to have fairly specific labeling in the MS, but there are clearly many cells shown in the tSNE that fall within cells kept for “LS”. Similar things may be said about Col6a1 or Nrn1/etc. The converse is also true: based on the same Allen Brain in situ images, Sst and Calb1 are also expressed in the medial septum, so it is unclear if cells kept in the “LS” clusters would include those. Reporting additional top genes for the clusters may help the reader better determine the potential for non-LS cells to be represented in the tSNE. Right now, the most important aspect of these data to me are Figure 1C, but this depends on the relative inclusion/exclusion of cells as discussed above.
---After excluding the “non-LS” cells in the tSNE, the authors then note what I assume are the top genes for each cluster. This strategy seems flawed to me because the clusters shown are formed relative to the expression of genes in the “non-LS” clusters when they were present. In other words, if the authors excluded the cells of the “non-LS” cells first then generated the tSNE (just as they did for transitioning from Supplemental 1 to Figure 1), do the authors think that the clustering for only “LS” cells would be similar? I suspect not, because these clusters already factor in the MS cells/etc.
---Only in the methods do the authors note these data are acquired from male mice. It should be clearly stated in the title or abstract that all of the data were collected from male mice.
---The authors state that the data shown only include animals with optical fibers above the target regions in the final analyses, but some of the current images make me uncertain about the accuracy of this (see Figure 5V). Similarly, it is unclear how much spread or specificity there may be in some of these injections/viruses. For example, there appears to be a lot of viral expression in the dorsal regions of the LS in CB-Cre mice. Are these terminals from ventral Calb1 cells? Are there more dorsally expressed Calb1 than is appreciated in the immunohistochemistry experiments? Also, several experiments use atlas schematics to represent the injections for the experiments, but no (or only partial) representative images are shown of injection sites. In Supplementary Figure 16e/h, there appears to be considerable expression of virus in regions above the POA, in what appears to be the BNST. The authors do not note the BNST in output terminals of the other figures. Are these from the LS? If not the LS, where are they from? My confidence may be bolstered by including more images of injections/placements (could be supplementary) and/or documenting viral spread/fiber placements. Perhaps the authors should note the number of exclusions based on hits/misses. Additionally, others have looked at outputs of Sst cells from the LS (Besnard et al. 2019), and there is no discussion of how their mapping compares (for example, no SUM is shown).
---The authors state: “The opposing effects of these pathways on social memory may be explained by the predominately GABAergic nature of AHN neuorns and the predominately glutamateric nature of LHA neurons.” GABAergic neurons are widely expressed within the LHA. Moreover, the inputs/outputs of the AHN vs. LHA may be quite distinct. There are many citations that could potentially be included here. I recommend a more thorough discussion here.
---Others have performed rabies tracing of Sst neurons of the LS (Besnard et al. 2019)—there is no discussion of how the authors’ findings compare with this work. This seems insufficient. Did the authors see the same inputs and at a similar level?
---Do Calb1 neurons overlap with Esr1 neurons?
MINOR ITEMS:
---I believe the dissection of the LS for snRNAseq requires more details (rather than simply referring to a separate paper that sequenced a different structure). How much tissue was collected? Was an equivalent amount of tissue collected from each animal? The LS is a long, bilateral structure, how were the authors able to determine coverage or specificity to the LS?
---It doesn’t bother me, as it is just a stylistic choice, but some of the legends are incredibly lengthy, perhaps they could be shortened by adding some of the information in the main text.
---In general, the authors found the majority of their circuit manipulations to only have effects on social behavior when manipulated during training/encoding but not when manipulated at test. If the authors then added a new animal after the test, do they expect to eliminate secondary discrimination? If so, this may bolster the argument towards specificity to encoding.
---I realize the authors report the number of cells, but can the authors report the number of mice from which the cells are derived in the slice electrophysiology experiments?
---Have the authors tried using a reporter line (crossing CB-Cre with the reporter line) to match what was seen with the immunohistochemistry preparations?
---Is there concern for ArchT being used in the terminal inhibition experiments? There is some evidence that sustained light activation of ArchT actually increases synaptic release at terminals: Mahn et al. 2016 Nature Neuroscience.
---There may be some typos in the text for which figure is being referred to.
---The authors state in the abstract: “While the hippocampus is crucial for social memory, the dynamic regulation of social memory, particularly the negative regulation, remains unclear.” I’m unsure what the authors mean by “negative” regulation, as this sounds like valence (especially since they do not see changes in RTRPP with Sst/CB). Can the authors clarify?

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We sincerely thank the reviewers for their insightful and constructive comments. In response, we have performed additional experiments, re-analyzed data, and expanded our discussion to address the points raised. With their valuable input, the clarity and overall quality of our manuscript have been greatly improved.
Point-to-point responses:
(Reviewers’ comments in Blue; Our responses in Black)

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
This study investigated the two parallel downstream circuits of ventral CA1, which has been shown to be the center of social memory, that are critical for social memory acquisition but not for social memory retrieval. The involvement of two circuits, vCA1d-SST+-dLS-lateral hypothalamic area and vCA1v-CB+-vLS-anterior hypothalamic nucleus, has been beautifully demonstrated using chemogenetic/optogenetic manipulation and electrophysiology. The results are very clear and strongly support the conclusions, so it is a study of exceptionally high scientific value to understand neural mechanisms underlying social memory. I have several concerns and suggestions to improve the paper.
Response: Thanks for your positive comments and insightful suggestions.
1. While there is no doubt that the brain region referred to as vCA1v is indeed vCA1, the region referred to as vCA1d is unclear from the coronal section whether it is CA1 or CA2. This is particularly important because dLS receives especially strong neural projections from the CA2 region, making it necessary to clarify this point. Therefore, in addition to the coronal sections, horizontal sections should be shown, and co-staining with CA2 marker genes such as RGS14 should be conducted.
Response: We appreciate your constructive comment very much. To test whether SST+-dLS neurons receive monosynaptic inputs from CA2 neurons, we have conducted additional RV tracing experiments and performed immunostaining for RGS14, a molecular marker of CA2 neurons, in horizontal hippocampal slices (Supplementary Fig. 19, revised manuscript). We found that RGS14+/GFP+ neurons account for 10.64% ± 1.39% of RGS14+ CA2 neurons, indicating that a subset of CA2 neurons projects to SST+-dLS neurons. However, RGS14+/GFP+ neurons represent only 3.12% ± 0.17% of all GFP+ input neurons in the hippocampus, suggesting that CA2 provides a relatively minor contribution to the total excitatory input to SST+-dLS neurons. Given that vCA1 neurons receive direct inputs from dorsal CA2 region1, we speculate that SST+-dLS neurons might also receive indirect input from CA2 neurons through a dCA2→vCA1→LS pathway. We have updated this notion in the revised manuscript (Result section, lines 357-364; Discussion section, lines 608-611).

2. Some of the data in this paper are related to the following study recently published in eLife. It is necessary to clearly highlight the differences between the two in the discussion section and to cite the study appropriately.
“A ventral hippocampal-lateral septum pathway regulates social novelty preference. Rashid et al., https://elifesciences.org/reviewed-preprints/97259”
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. Rashid et al. reported that inhibition of the vHPC→LS→ VTA pathway abolished social novelty preference2. In contrast, our study identified the vCA1d→ SST⁺–dLS→LHA and vCA1v→CB⁺–vLS→AHN pathways as two distinct hippocampal–septal– hypothalamic circuits that bidirectionally regulate social memory.
In our anterograde tracing experiments, we observed minimal GFP⁺ axonal projections from SST⁺ and CB⁺ LS neurons to the VTA (Supplementary Fig. 23a-c, revised manuscript), suggesting these populations do not significantly contribute to the vHPC→LS→VTA pathway. Furthermore, Rashid et al. demonstrated that VTA-projecting LS neurons receive inputs from both dCA1 and vCA12, whereas our data demonstrate that SST⁺–dLS and CB⁺–vLS neurons receive strong input primarily from vCA1, not from dCA1(see new Supplementary Fig. 17a-b, revised manuscript).
Previous studies have demonstrated that Esr1⁺ neurons in the LS send dense projections to the VTA and are implicated in reward seeking behaviors3. We therefore speculate that Esr1⁺ LS neurons may underlie the vHPC→LS→VTA circuit described by Rashid et al., whereas the SST⁺ and CB⁺ LS neurons characterized in our study form separate circuits that regulate social memory via hypothalamic targets. We have now incorporated this comparison and citation into the revised Discussion section (Discussion section, lines 622-628).
3. Regarding Figure 4 and Supplementary Figure 11, the SST+ neurons and CB+ neurons are shown to inhibit each other bilaterally. It is also suggested that they contribute to social memory performance as shown in Figure 8, partially supported by the SST+ (but not CB+) neurons contributing to enhanced theta oscillations (Figure 3) and presynaptic potentiation in vCA1d-SST+-dLS (but not in vCA1v-CB+-vLS) (Figure 6). This seems to indicate that positive regulation by SST+ neurons is stronger than negative regulation by CB+ neurons. Could the authors discuss these asymmetric results more, possibly from the viewpoint of the balance between bilateral inhibition? Furthermore, given the presynaptic potentiation in vCA1d-SST+-dLS, the results that vCA1-LS pathways are not important for social memory retrieval are counterintuitive. What could be the potential mechanism to explain this?
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments. We agree that the asymmetric influence of SST⁺ and CB⁺ neurons is a compelling observation that warrants further discussion. Based on our current dataset (Fig. 6), the vCA1d→SST⁺–dLS circuit undergoes selective synaptic potentiation during social memory acquisition, whereas no significant changes are observed in the vCA1v→CB⁺–vLS pathway. This synaptic asymmetry likely increases the responsiveness of SST⁺–dLS neurons to vCA1 input, thereby enhancing their functional influence relative to other LS subpopulations. Furthermore, due to the observed mutual inhibition between SST⁺ and CB⁺ neurons (Fig. 4g-j; Supplementary Fig. 15, revised manuscript), increased activity of SST⁺ neurons may further suppress CB⁺ neuron firing via lateral inhibition, thus amplifying the functional impact of the SST⁺ population during the memory acquisition.
We propose that SST⁺ and CB⁺ neurons work in a dynamically balanced manner to stabilize social memory formation. Their mutual inhibition may serve as a homeostatic mechanism that prevents memory from becoming either excessively rigid or unstable. Conceptually, these two neuronal populations may act similarly to a gas and brake system in a vehicle—SST⁺ neurons acting as the accelerator to promote memory encoding, and CB⁺ neurons serving as the brake to regulate or constrain it. The relative strength of these pathways may shift dynamically depending on behavioral demands.
Regarding the question of why the potentiated vCA1d→SST⁺–dLS pathway does not appear to contribute to social memory retrieval, we speculate that activation of SST⁺–dLS neurons and their downstream targets do not directly drive social exploration behavior (Supplementary Fig. 11c, revised manuscript). We hypothesize that social memory is a multi-phase process involving coordinated plasticity across distributed circuits, and further studies will be required to clarify the retrieval-specific plasticity mechanisms.
We have incorporated this interpretation into the revised manuscript (Discussion section, lines 576-583).
4. The authors showed that the vCA1-LS circuit is important for social memory acquisition but not recall, and the vCA1-NAc circuit is important for social memory recall but not acquisition (Supplementary Figure 15). According to Gergues et al. (Nature Neuroscience 23:1444, 2020), it has been shown that there are many neurons projecting to both LS and NAc. Are these dual-projecting neurons involved in social memory regulation shown in this study? Or are the single-projecting neurons involved?
Response: Thank you for this insightful question. As reported by Gergues et al., vCA1 region projects to both LS and NAc, including neurons that project exclusively to LS, exclusively to NAc, and a small subset that project to both regions4. A previous study also showed that NAc-projecting neurons are mainly located in vCA1v (see Fig. S3 in Okuyama, T., et al., Science, 2016)5. To estimate the percentage of dual-projecting vCA1 neurons targeting both NAc and vLS, we performed retrograde tracing by injecting CTB-555 into the NAc and CTB-488 into the vLS, and examined retrogradely labeled neurons in the vCA1. Our results showed that 10.95%± 1.19% of LS-projecting vCA1 neurons (green) also send projections to NAc, and 15.82%± 1.24% of NAc-projecting vCA1 neurons (red) also send projections to LS (Supplementary Fig. 21a-d, revised manuscript), suggesting that only a small amount of vCA1 neurons simultaneously project to both brain regions. These findings suggest that dual-projecting neurons make up only a minor fraction of the total projection population.
These results, combined with previous findings, suggest that two largely non-overlapping groups of single-projecting vCA1 neurons form the vCA1→LS and vCA1→NAc pathways, which function in parallel to regulate social memory acquisition and recall, respectively. This interpretation has been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Result section, lines 424-435).

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
(Remarks to the Author):
In this study, Zhang et al. investigated the role of two distinctive LS subpopulations- SST- and CB-expressing LS neurons- in bidirectional control of social memory acquisition. Using single nucleus RNA sequencing and immunostaining, they observed that SST- and CB-expressing LS neurons have molecularly and anatomically distinctive characteristics. The authors then demonstrated that each population positively and negatively regulates social memory acquisition, respectively. Optogenetic experiments further highlighted that this regulation is specifically engaged in social memory acquisition, but not social memory recall or sociability per se. Notably, SST LS neurons play a critical role in regulating socially relevant theta oscillations. At the circuit level, the dorsal and ventral LS (dLS, vLS) receive inputs from distinct parts of the hippocampus along its dorsal-ventral axis. Circuit-specific optogenetic manipulation revealed that vCA1d>dLS and vCA1v>vLS pathway can control social memory acquisition in a bidirectional way, similar to the effects observed after manipulating SST- and CB-expressing neurons, predominantly located in dorsal and ventral part of LS, respectively. The authors went one step further to demonstrate that the LHA and AHN are critical downstream targets of SST-and CB-expressing LS neurons to regulate social memory acquisition. Overall, this study provides valuable information into how specific neuronal circuits connecting the hippocampus to LS influence the social memory process. However, inconsistencies in data hinder in-dept interpretation, and generating superficial conclusions, primarily based on the results from artificial manipulation, is insufficient to support publication at this time. To further improve the paper, more clarifications listed below would be helpful.
Response: Thanks for your positive comments and insightful suggestions.
Here are some specific comments:
1. In Figure 1, snRNA seq results show that SST- and CB-expressing LS neurons display distinct molecular profiles with different expression levels for Nts, Glp1r, Htr2c and Prlr. Has this result been confirmed using other methods, such as in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry?
Response: Thank you for your advice. To validate the snRNA-seq findings, we performed RNAscope in situ hybridization to assess the expression levels of Glp1r, Nts, Htr2c, and Prlr in LS neurons. We found that Glp1r expression was primarily localized to the dLS, with 65.69% ± 0.92% of all Sst+ neurons co-expressing Glp1r and 73.96% ± 0.63% of all Glp1r + neurons co-expressing Sst, suggesting a high overlapping between Sst and Glp1r (Supplementary Fig. 3a, revised manuscript). Additonally, 52.55% ± 2.40% of all Sst+ neurons co-expressed Nts and 64.42% ± 1.93% of all Nts + neurons co-expressing Sst, suggesting a moderate but specific overlap between Sst and Nts (Supplementary Fig. 3b, revised manuscript). In contrast, 70.52% ± 1.37% of all Calb1+ neurons co-expressed Htr2c and 63.88% ± 1.22% of all Htr2c+ neurons co-expressing Calb1, with minimal colabeling observed in Sst⁺ neurons (Supplementary Fig. 3c, revised manuscript). Similarly, 81.53% ± 3.50% of all Calb1+ neurons co-expressed Prlr and 72.99% ± 3.40% of all Prlr + neurons co-expressing Calb1, further supporting a specific overlap between Calb1 and Prlr (Supplementary Fig. 3d, revised manuscript).
These findings are consistent with the snRNA seq data, which indicated that SST+ neurons exhibit higher expression levels of Glp1r and Nts, whereas Htr2c and Prlr are more highly expressed in CB+ neurons. We have added these findings to the revised manuscript (Result section, lines 110-115).

2. The author claimed that previous studies demonstrated the ‘controversial’ role of the LS in social behaviors (line #55, 139), but it is unclear what it meant by ‘controversial’ in this context. Given the heterogeneity of LS cell types, several studies have been descriptive, focusing on different populations of LS and highlighting their functional relevance on different domains of social behaviors. These studies do not necessarily appear to be inconsistent or in disagreement (controversial) with each other. Please clarify this point.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We acknowledge that our use of the term “controversial” was imprecise. We agree that the LS are organized into different molecularly defined clusters, which differentially regulate different domains of social behaviors depending on the context. Rather than being contradictory, these studies collectively highlight the functional heterogeneity of the LS. We have updated this notion with more precise wording in the revised manuscript (Result section, lines 60-61).
3. Figure 3 shows that theta oscillation power is increased during both social bouts and non-social intervals. Is this LS theta oscillation still sustained even after the social stimuli are removed, or is it specifically engaged during the social context? The same question would be related to SST LS neurons: Is the proportion of theta phase-locked SST LS neurons unique to social contexts?
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful comment. To address whether LS theta oscillations are sustained beyond social engagement, we performed additional control experiments measuring LFPs and single-unit activity from SST+ neurons in the LS across three conditions: 10‑min social interaction, 20-min exploration of empty chamber, and 10-min exploration of a novel object (Supplementary Fig. 13a, revised manuscript). Our data show that theta power increased significantly during social interactions but returned to baseline levels after the social stimulus (i.e., the unfamiliar mouse) was removed (Supplementary Fig. 13b, revised manuscript). Notably, exposure to a novel object did not produce a similar increase in theta power, indicating that the effect is specific to social stimuli. In contrast, the proportion of theta phase-locked SST+ neurons remained elevated even after the theta power declined, suggesting that while theta oscillations are specifically enhanced during social engagement, the phase-locking of SST+ neurons may persist beyond the immediate social context (Supplementary Fig. 13c, revised manuscript).
We have added these findings to the revised manuscript (Result section, lines 251-257; Discussion section, lines 588-591).

4. What is the explanation for using continuous social interaction tests for 20 min in Figure 3, instead of separate sessions of sociability vs. social novelty, as used throughout the rest of the paper? Figure 3e shows consistent enhancement of theta rhythm oscillations between P1 and P4 with no statistical difference as the familiarity is developed. More evidence is needed to substantiate their claim, this is a key neural mechanism for social memory acquisitions (line #220).
Response: Thank you for raising this important point.
In Fig. 3, we employed a continuous 20-min social interaction session with a single social stimulus to capture the cumulative neural response to repeated exposure to the same conspecific, analogous to the sequential 10-min sociability and 10-min social novelty phases used elsewhere in the study. Because theta oscillation power is increased during both social bouts and non-social intervals (Fig. 3d-e). Therefore, we excluded S2 to enable more precise analysis of how neural activity evolves over time in response to one social stimulus. This rationale has been added to the revised manuscript (Result section, lines 230-232).
To determine whether the enhanced theta oscillations are specifically engaged by social context, we recorded LFP activity during a 10-min social interaction session (social context), followed by a 20-min session without social stimuli (empty context), and a 10-min novel object session (Supplementary Fig. 13a, revised manuscript). Theta power increased rapidly during the social session—beginning in the second 2-minute bin— and remained elevated throughout. In contrast, theta power remained at baseline during the empty context and object sessions (Supplementary Fig. 13b, revised manuscript). Our results suggest that enhanced theta oscillations are specific to social context, and it may represent a key neural mechanism for social memory acquisition.
We have included these new data and interpretations in the revised manuscript (Result section, lines 251-257; Discussion section, lines 588-591).
5. What is the justification for the lack of changes in the power of theta rhythm oscillations in response to 20 Hz-ChR2 activation of SST LS neurons in Figure 3m?
Response: Thank you for this important question. Previous work has shown that activation of fast-spiking GABAergic neurons at a given frequency can enhance the LFP power at the corresponding frequency (e.g., 40 Hz stimulation increases 40 Hz power; Cardin et al., 2009, see Figure 3)6. This indicates that the stimulation frequency strongly influences the resulting network oscillations.
To directly test this in the LS, we expressed ChR2 in SST+ neurons and applied photostimulation across a wide frequency range (5 to 160 Hz; see Revision Fig. 1a). Compared to baseline, stimulation between 10–80 Hz increased the normalized LFP power within ±2 Hz of the stimulation frequency (Revision Fig. 1a). Specifically, 10 Hz stimulation enhanced oscillations in the theta range (8–12 Hz), whereas 20 Hz stimulation increased power in the 18–22 Hz band (Revision Fig. 1b-c). These results show that 20 Hz activation does not enhance theta power but instead drives oscillations closer to its own stimulation frequency. Thus, the lack of theta enhancement during 20 Hz stimulation in Fig. 3m is consistent with this frequency-specific effect and highlights that 10 Hz SST⁺ activation is particularly effective in promoting theta oscillations.

6. In Figure 5, TeNT silencing is applied to the vCA1d>dLS pathway using intersectional viral strategies. Given the collateral projections of vCA1 neurons, it is important to clarify whether the vCA1d>dLS pathway is a key participant for blocking the enhanced theta oscillations during social interaction in Supplementary Fig.14.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. To address the role of the vCA1d→dLS pathway in regulating theta oscillations during social interaction, we injected AAV-CamKⅡ-eArchT3.0-EGFP into the vCA1d of C57 mice, and implanted an LFP-recording optrode in the dLS to enable pathway-specific silencing during social behavior. Compared to baseline recordings without light stimulation, optogenetic inhibition of vCA1d→dLS pathway abolished the enhanced theta oscillations typically observed during social interaction (Supplementary Fig. 20e, revised manuscript). These results confirm that the vCA1d→dLS projection is necessary for the social interaction-driven increase in theta power.
We have incorporated these findings into the revised manuscript (Result section, lines 404-407).
